units.tr: If the things which Melchisedec offered (as they say) were not covered with an alien form and alien accidents, and in the sacrifice of the Mass (if the Papists' word is to be believed) Christ is offered covered with an alien form and alien accidents, how will the oblation of Melchisedec pertain to the sacrifice of the Mass? For if what appears is what is offered in the Mass, then certainly bread and wine are offered in the Mass; if something else appears and something else is offered in the Mass, then you clearly depart far from Melchisedec. For I press the word brought forth, which Moses uses when he tells that Melchisedec brought forth bread and wine. But it is one thing to bring something openly into view, and quite another to veil and cover that very thing so that it is not open to the eyes. Likewise:

units.la: Si panem & vinum obtulit Melchisedecus (ut Pontificij contendunt) certè hæc non fuit oblatio pro peccatis, sed Eucharistica & gratiarum actionis. Sic enim ille: Benedictus Deus excelsus qui tradidit hostes tuos in manum tuam. Itaque sequeretur ex ipsorum Pontificiorum argumento: Missæ sacrificium esse tantùm εὐχαριστικόν, non autem propitiatorium pro peccatis. Item.
units.tr: "If Melchisedec offered bread and wine" (as the Papists contend), then certainly this was not an offering for sins but a eucharistic offering, a thanksgiving. For he says: Blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand. So it would follow from the Papists' own argument that the sacrifice of the Mass is merely eucharistic and not propitiatory for sins. Again.

units.la: Ex iis quæ passus est didicit obedientiam: Et consummatus factus est autor salutis æternæ omnibus qui ipsi auscultant: cognominatus à Deo Pontifex secundùm ordinem Melchisedec (inquit Apostolus) Cum igitur Christus non fuerit consummatus in sacra Cœna: certè non fuit cognominatus sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedec respectu sacræ Cœnæ, quemadmodum Pontificij falsò tradiderunt. Sed de his hactenus: pleraque enim huiusmodi afferri possent.
units.tr: He learned obedience from what he suffered; and, being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being named by God a High Priest after the order of Melchisedec, as the Apostle says. Therefore, since Christ was not made perfect in the Lord's Supper, he certainly was not named a priest after the order of Melchisedec with respect to the Lord's Supper, as the Papists have falsely taught. But let this be enough on these points, for many such things could be brought forward.

units.la: Corrigamus igitur errorem Pontificiorū hoc modo:
units.tr: Let us therefore correct the error of the Papists in this way:

units.la: Quandoquidem Melchisedeci cum Christo collatio, non temere & humano arbitratu, sed ex ipsa Scriptura depromenda est: ita statuere debemus: Melchisedecum gessisse figuram Christi, quòd fuerit rex simul & sacerdos, quòd proponatur tanquam æternus, denique quòd maior fuerit Abra-hamo, ac proinde Leuiticis sacerdotibus ipsius Abrahami posteris. Id quod perspi-cuum est, tum quia Abrahamo benedixit, tū quia accepit decimas ab Abrahamo. Ex hac autem collatione efficitur: Christum sacerdotem secundùm ordinem Melchisedec, etiam adhibito iureiurando à Deo constitutum, omnibus Leuiticis sacerdotibus esse longè superiorem: in quo uno sacerdotium remansit, adeò, ut neque Pontificij sacerdotes posint, nec ipsum Missæ sacrificium constitui, quin Christus de suo æterno sacerdotio deturbetur: quod absit.
units.tr: Since the comparison of Melchisedec with Christ is not to be drawn carelessly or at human whim, but from Scripture itself, we ought to hold as follows: Melchisedec bore the figure of Christ in that he was at once king and priest, in that he is presented as eternal, and finally in that he was greater than Abraham, and therefore greater than the Levitical priests, who were Abraham's descendants. This is clear both because he blessed Abraham and because he received tithes from Abraham. From this comparison it follows that Christ, a priest after the order of Melchisedec, constituted by God even with an oath, is far superior to all the Levitical priests; and in him alone the priesthood remains. So it is that neither Papist priests nor the sacrifice of the Mass itself can be set up without Christ's eternal priesthood being thrown down, which God forbid.

units.la: Obiectio 10.
units.tr: Objection 10.

units.la: Ab ortu Solis usque ad Occasum magnum est nomen meum in Gentibus & in omni loco sacrificatur & offertur nomini meo oblatio munda: quia magnum est nomen meum in Gentibus: dicit Dominus exercituum. Hæc Malachias. Ergo sacrificium Missæ est legitimum. Consequentia patet: quia munda illa oblatio quam dicit offerendam in omni loco, non potest aliter intelligi iuxta mentem Prophetæ, quàm de mundissima oblatione corporis & sanguinis Christi quæ in omni loco offertur, videlicet, in sacrificio Missæ: quemadmodum Malachias prophetavit.
units.tr: From the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering; for my name is great among the Gentiles, says the Lord of hosts. These are the words of Malachi. Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass is lawful. The consequence is plain, because that pure offering which he says is to be offered in every place cannot, according to the mind of the Prophet, be understood otherwise than of the most pure offering of the body and blood of Christ, which is offered in every place, namely in the sacrifice of the Mass, as Malachi prophesied.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Consequens est salsissimum. Error: Petitio principij. Quis enim illis concesserit, Missæ obla-
units.tr: The consequence is most absurd. It is an error: begging the question. For who would have granted them that the offering of the Mass

units.la: oblationem mundam esse? Plana est autem Malachiae sententia de spirituali Dei cultu differentis, qui potissimum eluxit Ecclesiae Christianae temporibus, quum Gentes Evangelicam praedicationem amplexae sunt. Eò spectant haec verba, Magnum nomen meum in Gentibus, bis repetita; qui mos Hebraeorum est, ut id quod proponunt, melius inculcent. Huc adde: Ab ortu Solis, usque ad Occasum, itemque: In omni loco, inquit. Legalis enim Dei cultus unius Gentis finibus continebatur, & ipsa externa sacrificia in uno tantum loco fiebant ex verbo Dei. Quare manifestus est sensus huius Prophetiae: quae nihil habet cum Missae sacrificio commune.
units.tr: is a pure offering? The meaning of Malachi is plain, however, as he speaks of the spiritual worship of God, which chiefly shone forth in the times of the Christian Church, when the Gentiles embraced the evangelical preaching. To this point refer these words, My name is great among the Gentiles, repeated twice, which is the manner of the Hebrews, to impress more strongly what they set forth. Add to this: from the rising of the sun to its setting, and likewise: in every place, he says. For the legal worship of God was confined within the bounds of one nation, and the external sacrifices were performed in only one place by the word of God. Hence the sense of this prophecy is manifest, and it has nothing in common with the sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: At, inquis, meminit sacrificij & oblationis. Ut respondeam: primum recitabo locum Malachiae ex Hebraico contextu, tum excutiam quantum valeat haec obiectio. In omni loco, inquit, incensum oblatum nomini meo, & oblatio munda. Haec ille: utitur autem vocabulo, Mincha, quo certum aliquod legalis oblationis genus significabatur, ut videre licet apud Moysen. Omnia igitur haec vocabula ad legalem cultum proprie pertinent.
units.tr: But, you say, it mentions sacrifice and offering. To answer: first I will recite the passage of Malachi from the Hebrew text, and then examine how much this objection is worth. In every place, he says, incense is offered to my name, and a pure offering. So he says; and he uses the word Mincha [מנחה], by which a certain kind of legal offering was signified, as may be seen in Moses. All these words therefore properly pertain to the legal worship.

units.la: Iam attendamus quorsum euadat Pontificiorum argumentum. Meminit Malachias incensi & oblationis Minchae: praedixit igitur futurum Missae sacrificium. Cedo mihi μέσον huiusce Conclusionis. Qui dicit incensum & oblationem, is-ne, obsecro, dicit Missæ sacrificium? Ecce, igitur, vides te nihil posse ex Malachia efficere, nisi ante demonstraueris, sacrificium Missæ esse illud incensum & illam ipsam oblationē de qua Malachias locutus est: atque ita, qui tibi videbaris metam attingere, hæres adhuc in ipsis carceribus.
units.tr: Let us now consider where the Papists' argument leads. Malachi mentions incense and the offering of Mincha; therefore he foretold the future sacrifice of the Mass. Show me the middle term of this conclusion! Tell me, I beg you, does one who speaks of incense and offering therefore speak of the sacrifice of the Mass? Behold, then, you see that you can draw nothing from Malachi unless you first demonstrate that the sacrifice of the Mass is that very incense and that very offering of which Malachi spoke; and so you, who seemed to yourself to be reaching the goal, remain stuck in the starting gates.

units.la: Secundus error παρὰ τὸν ὁμωνυμίαν. Cùm enim vocabula quibus vtitur Malachias varie accipi posint, & sint ἐκ τῶν πολλαχῶς λεγομένων (possunt enim accipi, vel proprie, vel figuratè) isti tamen ea perinde accipiunt, ac si rem vnam tantùm significarent. Quare iam obruamus incommodis ineptam illam Conclusionem, & ipsos Pontificios deprehendamus ἐν ἀντιφάσει, hoc modo:
units.tr: A second error, through equivocation. For since the words Malachi uses can be taken in various ways, and are from things said in many ways (for they may be taken either properly or figuratively), these people nevertheless take them as though they signified only one thing. Therefore let us now overthrow that absurd conclusion with its disadvantages, and catch the Papists in a contradiction, in this way:

units.la: I Nomina intensi & oblationis à Malachia usurpata, aut intelligenda sunt proprie: aut, metaphoricè: si proprie: ergo Malachias de cultu legali locutus esset, ac proinde locus hic ad noui Testamenti tempora non pertineret. Si metaphoricè: & illa nomina de Missa intelligenda sunt. Ergo Missa est sacrificium metaphoricè dictum: ac propterea non reale, verum & externum sacrificium: quod tamen illi affirmant: aut, Proprie dictum, &, Metaphoricè dictum idem sunt nec vlla ratione distinguuntur. Ἀδιώατον.
units.tr: The names of incense and offering used by Malachi must be understood either properly or metaphorically. If properly, then Malachi would have spoken of legal worship, and so this passage would not pertain to the times of the New Testament. If metaphorically, then those names must be understood of the Mass. Therefore the Mass is a sacrifice spoken of metaphorically, and so not a real, true and external sacrifice; yet they affirm this. Or else, "properly spoken" and "metaphorically spoken" are the same and are not distinguished by any reasoning. Impossible.

units.la: Reuocent igitur in memoriā quo pacto nobis explicarint homonymiam vocabuli sacrisacrificij: nimirum, sacrificium metaphori-cè dictum, significare cultum interiorem & ea quae spectant ad vitae sanctimoniam: Missam autem esse sacrificium externum & proprie dictum. Haec, inquam, secum repu-tent: ac tum dent operam suis argumentis conciliandis. Item.
units.tr: Let them therefore call to mind how they have explained to us the homonymy of the word sacrifice: namely, that a sacrifice spoken of metaphorically signifies inner worship and the things that pertain to the holiness of life, while the Mass is an external sacrifice spoken of properly. These things, I say, let them consider with themselves, and then take pains to reconcile their arguments. Again.

units.la: Si incensum ad novi Testamenti tempora relatum, ipsis Apostolis interpretibus, nunquam de externo incenso, semper autem de spirituali cultu intelligendum est: idem profecto de oblatione Mincha dicendum erit: propter contextum orationis, & utriusque vocabuli coniunctionem.
units.tr: If incense, referred to the times of the New Testament, must always be understood, as the Apostles themselves interpret it, not of external incense but of spiritual worship, the same must certainly be said of the offering of Mincha, on account of the context of the passage and the conjunction of the two words.

units.la: Atque ita locus Malachiae de spirituali cultu intelligendus erit. Quem si velint sua Missae accommodare: externo igitur sacrificio renuntient necesse est: aut, externum, & internum, idem erunt. Ἀδιάφορον.
units.tr: And so the passage of Malachi must be understood of spiritual worship. If they wish to apply it to their Mass, they must necessarily renounce an external sacrifice; or else the external and the internal will be the same. Indifferent.

units.la: Assumptum patet inductione. Data sunt illi, inquit Ioannes, incensa multa ut daret de orationibus sanctorum omnium super altare aureum quod est ante thronum. Et ascendit fumus incensorum de orationibus sanctorum. &c.
units.tr: The assumption is clear by induction. There were given to him, says John, many incense offerings, that he should give them with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne. And the smoke of the incense rose with the prayers of the saints, etc.

units.la: Habentes singuli citharas & phialas aureas plenas suffitum quae sunt preces sanctorum.
units.tr: Each one having harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.

units.la: Accepi ab Epaphrodito quae a vobis missa sunt, odorem bonae fragrantiae, inquit Paulus, & quaecunque eo spectant, ferant Pontificij εὐ-θασιν, si posint. Item.
units.tr: I have received from Epaphroditus what was sent by you, the odour of a sweet fragrance, says Paul; and whatever pertains to that, let the Papists bear it as a sweet-smelling savour [εὐωδίας], if they can. Again.

units.la: Si quia Malachias de temporibus novi Testamenti verba faciens, mentionem fecit incensi & oblationis Mincha, idcirco externa quædam & realis oblatio constituenda est: Ergo simili ratione quia Esaias de his ipsis temporibus verba faciens prædixit fideles ascensuros in montem Sion, aliquid tale constituendum erit in Ecclesia Christiana. Item.
units.tr: If, since Malachi, speaking of the times of the New Testament, made mention of incense and the offering of Mincha, therefore some external and real offering must be established. Then by the same reasoning, since Isaiah, speaking of these same times, foretold that the faithful would ascend to the mountain of Zion, something of that kind must be established in the Christian Church. Again.

units.la: Quia idem Propheta prædixit fore vt veri Israëlitæ offerantur Deo tanquam oblatio Mincha, idq; Hierosolymæ super montem sanctum Domini: idcirco ipsi homines erunt externo sacrificio & externa oblatione Deo offerendi. Item.
units.tr: Since the same Prophet foretold that true Israelites would be offered to God as a Mincha offering, and that in Jerusalem, upon the holy mountain of the Lord, therefore men themselves will have to be offered to God by an external sacrifice and an external oblation. Again.

units.la: Quia idem Propheta amplitudinem Ecclesiæ Christianæ describens, prædixit futurum, vt porta ciuitatis Hierusalem nunquam claudantur, vt illuc afferatur fortitudo Gentium, &c. idcirco Hierosolyma quædam externa & terrestris erit hodie constituenda. Item.
units.tr: Since the same Prophet, describing the extent of the Christian Church, foretold that the gate of the city of Jerusalem would never be shut, that the strength of the Gentiles would be brought there, etc., therefore some external and earthly Jerusalem must today be established. Again.

units.la: Quia Zacharias ages de Christiana Ecclesia temporibus dixit futurũ vt fideles ascendant Hierosolymam, festum Tabernaculorum celebraturi, & ibi sacrificent, & carnes coquant in lebetibus, &c. idcirco res eiusmodi sunt in Ecclesiam Christianam renocãda. Quæ omnia quis non videt esse ἀδωάλα & absurda? Nec Pontificij rationem vllam dissimilitudinis proferre possunt.
units.tr: Since Zechariah, speaking of the times of the Christian Church, said that the faithful would go up to Jerusalem to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles, and would sacrifice there and boil the flesh in pots, etc., therefore things of that kind must be restored to the Christian Church. Who does not see that all these things are absurd and ridiculous? Nor can the Papists bring forward any reason for the dissimilarity.

units.la: Atenim, inquiunt, Si locus Malachiæ de spirituali oblatione exponatur, quomodo dicetur munda oblatio? vos enim ipsi dicitis, etiam piorum opera immunda esse.Respondeo Malachiam opponere mundam illam oblationem, de qua loquitur, Iudæorum peccatis, qui sacrificia non ita uti decebat, offerebant. At vos, inquit, polluistis ipsum videlicet nomen meum &c. Quare cultus Dei exhibitus secundum verbum ipsius, per se mundus est. Quanuis autem in fidelibus multæ adhuc maculæ hæreant: quia tamen sacrificia spiritualia offerunt Deo per Christum, qui suo sanguine Ecclesiam mundauit ut eam sisteret sine macula & ruga, inquit Apostolus: ideo piorum oblatio munda est. Sic enim Apostolus ad Heb. Peripsum Christum, inquit, assidue offeramus Deo sacrificium laudis. Et Petrus, Ipsi quoque velut vivi lapides ædificamini, inquit, domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offerendum spirituales hostias acceptas Deo per Iesum Christum. Et Paulus dicit se esse Ministrum apud Gentes, Ut oblatio Gentium fiat accepta, sanctificata per Spiritum Sanctum. Et alibi. Velim, inquit, viros precari in quovis loco puras manus attollentes. Itemque Ut sisistis, inquit, corpora vestra hostiam vivam, sanctam, acceptam Deo. Atque ut ad Prophetas reuertamur: Quum Esaias prophetat de hominibus Deo per Euangelij prædicationem offerendis, ait perinde id fore, ut si oblatio Mincha Deo in mundo vase offeratur.
units.tr: But, they say, if the passage of Malachi is expounded of a spiritual offering, how will it be called a pure offering? For you yourselves say that even the works of the pious are unclean. I answer that Malachi sets against that pure offering of which he speaks the sins of the Jews, who offered sacrifices otherwise than was fitting. But you, he says, have polluted it, that is, my name, etc. Therefore the worship of God rendered according to his word is in itself pure. Although many stains still cling to the faithful, nevertheless, because they offer spiritual sacrifices to God through Christ, who by his blood cleansed the Church so as to present it without spot or wrinkle, as the Apostle says, the offering of the pious is pure. For thus the Apostle to the Hebrews: Through him, he says, let us continually offer to God the sacrifice of praise. And Peter: You also, he says, as living stones, are built up a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. And Paul says that he is a minister among the Gentiles, that the offering of the Gentiles may be made acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. And elsewhere: I desire, he says, that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands. And again: that you present your bodies, he says, a living, holy sacrifice, acceptable to God. And to return to the Prophets: when Isaiah prophesies of men to be offered to God through the preaching of the gospel, he says that it will be as if a Mincha offering were offered to God in a clean vessel.

units.la: Verum enim uero, inquiunt, loquitur Malachias de re sæpius facienda, quandoquidem vsurpat tempus præsens: quū dicit, Offertur.
units.tr: "But surely," they say, "Malachi speaks of something to be done often, since he uses the present tense when he says, It is offered."

units.la: Gentes autem semel vocatæ sunt. Primum inepta est hæc ratiocinatio. Nam si velint hanc Prophetiam ad tempora noui Testamenti referre: necessario dicendum erit, præsens tempus pro futuro vsurpari: atque ita rem significari aliquanto pòst futuram, fuit enim Malachias Prophetarum vltimus, ac proinde omniù proximus salutiferæ Christi exhibitioni. Præterea, non restringimus hanc Prophetiam ad primam illam vocationem Gentium, quum primùm illis oblata fuit Euangelij prædicatio (quod tamen nondum etiam plane absolutum est) sed eá generaliter intelligimus, de spirituali cultu & de spiritualibus Christianorū sacrificiis, quæ omnia vno oblationis nomine significauit Malachias: vt quum Psaltes dixit, Sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, omnia legalia sacrificia, & omnes legales oblationes intellexit. Et Paulus ea omnia quæ ad piorum sanctimoniam carnisque mortificationem pertinent, vocauit, hostiam viuam, sanctam, acceptam Deo & cultum rationalem.
units.tr: This argument is weak in the first place. If they want to refer this prophecy to the times of the New Testament, they must say that the present tense is used for the future, and so the thing signified would be some time in the future. Malachi was the last of the Prophets and therefore the nearest of all to the saving manifestation of Christ. Moreover, we do not restrict this prophecy to the first calling of the Gentiles, when the preaching of the gospel was first offered to them (which in any case is not yet fully completed). We understand it generally, of spiritual worship and of the spiritual sacrifices of Christians, all of which Malachi signified by the one name of offering. Just as when the Psalmist said, Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, he meant all the legal sacrifices and all the legal offerings. And Paul called all those things that pertain to the holiness of the godly and the mortification of the flesh a living, holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, and a reasonable service.

units.la: Retorqueamus locum hunc in Pontificios, hoc modo.
units.tr: Let us turn this passage back against the Papists, in this way.

units.la: 1 Nihil quod destituitur verbo Dei, oblatio munda esse potest.
units.tr: 1. Nothing that is destitute of the Word of God can be a pure offering.

units.la: Missa sacrificium destituitur verbo Dei. (vt patuit ex superioribus.)
units.tr: The sacrifice of the Mass is destitute of the Word of God (as was shown above).

units.la: Quare Missa sacrificium oblatio munda esse non potest. Et vi Consequentis locus Malachiæ de Missæ sacrificio non est intelligendus. Item.
units.tr: Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass cannot be a pure offering. And by the force of the consequence, the passage of Malachi is not to be understood of the sacrifice of the Mass. Likewise:

units.la: 2 Si oblatio Mincha de qua loquitur Malachias intelligenda est de Missæ sacrificio (ut Pontifici flagitant) certè in Missæ sacrificio offertur panis, non autem corpus Christi.
units.tr: 2. If the offering of the meal (Mincha) of which Malachi speaks is to be understood of the sacrifice of the Mass (as the Papists insist), then certainly in the sacrifice of the Mass bread is offered, not the body of Christ.

units.la: Consequentia patet: quia Mincha proprie significabat rerum inanimatarum oblationem, ut constat ex Leuitic. 2. &c. Quamobrem hunc Pontificiorum errorem corrigamus & Malachiam ab eorum falsa interpretatione vindicemus, in hunc modum:
units.tr: The consequence is plain, because Mincha properly signified the offering of inanimate things, as is clear from Leviticus 2, and so on. Therefore let us correct this error of the Papists, and vindicate Malachi from their false interpretation, in this way:

units.la: Quum Malachias Iudæorum vitia, rerumque sacrarum contemptum grauissimè reprehenderet, & spiritualem Dei cultum in Ecclesia Christiana futurum, adeoque ipsam Gentium vocationem prædiceret: allusit ad legales cæremonias, & earum vocabulis vsus est, nempe incenso & oblatione Mincha: Qui Prophetarum mos est: & quod adeo ipsi etiam Malachiæ paulò post vsuuenit, ita de noui Testamenti temporibus loquenti. Filios, inquit, Leui emundabit & excoquet vt aurum & argentum, & offerent Domino oblationem Mincha in iustitia, & accepta erit Domino oblatio Iuda & Hierusalem, vt diebus antiquis & annis prioribus. Quàobrem incensi & oblationis nominibus intellexit cultum illum, quem fideles post aduentum Christi iussi sunt exhibere Deo.
units.tr: When Malachi was most severely rebuking the sins of the Jews and their contempt for sacred things, and was foretelling the spiritual worship that would be in the Christian Church, and therefore the very calling of the Gentiles, he alluded to the legal ceremonies and used their names, namely incense and the offering of Mincha. This is the custom of the Prophets, and it happened even to Malachi himself a little later, when he spoke of the times of the New Testament: He will purify, he says, the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they shall offer to the Lord an offering of Mincha in righteousness, and the offering of Judah and Jerusalem shall be acceptable to the Lord, as in the days of old and in former years. Therefore by the names of incense and offering he understood that worship which the faithful, after the coming of Christ, were commanded to render to God.

units.la: Cùm autem nullum externum & reale sacrificium Christus in Ecclesia Christiana instituerit: locus hic Malachiæ ad commentitium Missæ sacrificium detorqueri nō potest: quem nos ex scriptis Apostolicis, non autem ex humanis somniis, exponere atque intelligere debemus.
units.tr: Since Christ instituted in the Christian Church no external and real sacrifice, this passage of Malachi cannot be twisted into the invented sacrifice of the Mass. We must expound and understand it from the apostolic writings, not from human dreams.

units.la: Obiectio II.
units.tr: Objection II.

units.la: Vos autem sacerdotes Dei vocabimini, inquit Esaias. Et rursus: Assumam ex eis in Sacerdotes & Leuitas. Item.
units.tr: But you, says Isaiah, shall be called priests of God. And again: I will take from them for priests and Levites. Likewise:

units.la: Adducam eos in montem sanctum meum & lætificabo eos in domo orationis meæ. Holocausta eorum & victimæ placebunt mihi super altari meo, &c. Ergo Missæ sacrificium est legitimum.
units.tr: I will bring them to my holy mountain and gladden them in my house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and sacrifices shall be pleasing to me on my altar, etc. Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass is lawful.

units.la: Consequentia patet. Nam hæ Prophetiæ de temporibus Ecclesiæ Christianæ intelligendæ sunt, in qua futuros esse sacerdotes, futuráque altaria Esaias prædixit: ac proinde futurum etiam externum sacrificium. Hoc enim postulat relatio inter Sacerdotes, altare, & ipsum sacrificium.
units.tr: The consequence is plain. For these prophecies must be understood of the times of the Christian Church, in which Isaiah foretold that there would be priests and altars; and therefore an external sacrifice too. For the relation between priests, altar and sacrifice requires this.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Fallit Consequentia. Error est: tum παρα τῳ ὁμωνυμίαν, tum etiam παρὰ τῶ ἀγνοίαν τῆ ἐλέγχε: nec enim eo modo sumunt vocabula, sacerdotis, & altaris, quo ab Esaia vsurpata sunt. Idem igitur plane respondeo quod supra: videlicet, cultum spiritualé futurū noui Testamenti temporibus ab Esaiæ proproponi figurate: idque, nominibus quae ad legalem cultum proprie spectabant, per allusionem vsurpatis. Quare superior refutatio in hanc etiam obiectionem quadrat. Etenim si nomina illa metaphorice accipienda sunt: nihil iuuant Missae sacrificium, quod illi externum & proprie dictum esse volunt. Ne mihi repetendum sit ex arte differendi διαλεκτικὸν τὰς μεταφορὰς, aut (quod forte illis futurum est gratius) proponendum hoc Scholasticorum dogma: Symbolicam Theologiam non esse argumentatiuam. Quod si nomina illa sint proprie accipienda: regredimur ergo ad Iudaeos, de caelesti in terrestre Hierosolymam deturbati. Iam igitur nobis tem plum Hierosolymitanum extruendum est, & erigendum altare, & sacerdotes e tribu Leui vndique conquirendi (si modo inueniri possint) vt ita iuxta locos illos Propheticos, non in omni loco (vt paulo ante ex Malachia efficere volebant) sed Hierosolymae tantum, & ad altare ibi constitutum, nec iam ab ista sacrificulorum turba promiscua, sed a solis Iudaeis e tribu Leui oriundis Missa celebratur.
units.tr: The consequence fails. The error is both a fallacy of equivocation [παρὰ τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν] and a fallacy of ignorance of the refutation [παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τοῦ ἐλέγχου]. For they do not take the words priest and altar in the sense in which Isaiah used them. So I answer exactly as above: namely, that Isaiah foreshadows figuratively the spiritual worship that would be in the times of the New Testament, and he uses names that properly belonged to the legal worship, by way of allusion. Hence my earlier refutation fits this objection too. For if those names are to be taken metaphorically, they do nothing to help the sacrifice of the Mass, which they want to be external and properly so called. I need not repeat here the art of disputing, to argue dialectically about metaphors [διαλεκτικὸν τὰς μεταφοράς], or (which perhaps will be more welcome to them) put forward this dogma of the Schoolmen: Symbolical theology is not argumentative. But if those names are to be taken properly, then we are led back to the Jews, cast down from the heavenly Jerusalem to the earthly one. Then we must build the temple at Jerusalem, erect the altar, and search out priests from the tribe of Levi on every side (if they can be found), so that, according to those prophetic passages, the Mass is celebrated not in every place (as a little earlier they tried to prove from Malachi) but only at Jerusalem and at the altar set up there, and not by this promiscuous crowd of little sacrificers, but only by Jews born of the tribe of Levi.

units.la: Significantur sacrificia, inquis: propter vocabulorum relationem. Respondeo: cum vocabula figurate vsurpentur: sacrificium quo que figurate esse intelligendum: idque, vi ipsius relationis. Hoc autem connexum: si est sacrificium, est igitur sacrificium extornum: fallit παρὰ τὸ ἐπιφαινόμενον. Nouum enim Testamentum habet sua sacrificia, nempe spiritualia, vt ante a nobis dictum est. Quam obrem (ne rem actam agere videamur) ita corrigamus falsas Pontificiorum interpretationes.
units.tr: You say the sacrifices are signified because of the relation of the words. I answer: when words are used figuratively, the sacrifice too must be understood figuratively, and that by the very force of the relation. But the connection, "if there is a sacrifice, then there is an external sacrifice," is a fallacy of appearance [παρὰ τὸ ἐπιφαινόμενον]. For the New Testament has its own sacrifices, namely spiritual ones, as was said before by us. Therefore (lest we seem to be going over old ground) let us correct in this way the false interpretations of the Papists.

units.la: Esaias de Christiana Ecclesia prophetas: Vos autem, inquit, sacerdotes Dei vocabimini: non de sacrificulis Pontificiis loquens: sed de piis omnibus, de quibus Petrus Esaiae interpres locupletissimus: Vos, inquit, genus electum, regale sacerdotium, &c. Nam apud Esaiam, qui non sunt sacerdotes appellandi, illi dicuntur alieni, & filij peregrinorum. Quam oppositionem Pontificij non animaduertunt. Idem Esaias praedixit noui Testamenti temporibus assumendos ex fidelibus sacerdotes Leuiticos (nec enim extat copula in contextu Hebraico) non quòd stare debeat sacerdotiū Leuiticū (est enim mutatum, inquit Apostolus,) sed ita significauit Esaias ministerium Euangelicum Leuitico succeßurum. Sic enim Paulus Getes sacrificabat Deo (vti ille ipse testis est) quū eas ad Euangelij cognitionem adducebat. Denique meminit Esaias Sionis, templi, holocaustorum & altaris, non vt in Ecclesia Christiana futurum aliquod externū sacrificium denotaret: (quis enim hęc vnquam iuxta literam, ac nō potius figuratē intelligat, nisi Iudaizet?) sed vt propositā legalium caeremoniarū imagine,
units.tr: Isaiah prophesies of the Christian Church: But you, he says, shall be called priests of God. He is not speaking of the Papist little sacrificers, but of all the godly, of whom Peter, the most thorough interpreter of Isaiah, says: You, he says, are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, etc. For in Isaiah those who are not to be called priests are called aliens and sons of foreigners. The Papists do not notice this opposition. The same Isaiah foretold that in the times of the New Testament priests of the Levitical kind would be taken from the faithful (for the copula does not stand in the Hebrew context), not because the Levitical priesthood ought to stand (for it has been changed, says the Apostle), but Isaiah thus signified that the Gospel ministry would succeed the Levitical. For so Paul sacrificed the Gentiles to God (as he himself is witness) when he led them to the knowledge of the gospel. Finally, Isaiah mentions Zion, the temple, the burnt offerings and the altar, not to denote some external sacrifice to be in the Christian Church (for who ever understands these things literally rather than figuratively, unless he is a Judaizer?), but to set before us the image of the legal ceremonies, so as to foreshadow the spiritual worship that would be in the Christian Church.

units.la: Esai.66. Rom.15. Ef.66. Ef.56. ne, cultum spiritualem in Ecclesia Christiana futurum adumbraret. Sic ille ipse Esaias prophetauit altare futurum in media Ægypto: de publica verae religionis professione, non autem de innumerabilibus Pontificiorum altaribus verba faciens. Sic alibi de cultu spirituali Ecclesiae Christianae differens:
units.tr: Isaiah 66. Romans 15. Ephesians 66. Ephesians 56. Thus the same Isaiah prophesied that there would be an altar in the midst of Egypt, speaking of the public profession of the true religion, not of the countless altars of the Papists. Likewise elsewhere, when he treats of the spiritual worship of the Christian Church:

units.la: Omnes oues Cedar congregabuntur tibi, inquit: arietes Nebaioth ministrabunt tibi: ascendent super altare meum ad beneplacitum, & domum maiestatis meae decorabo. Sic etiam Ioannes mentionem fecit caelestis altaris, thuribuli, suffitus, templi, atrij exterioris, ipsius etiam arcae foederis & aliorum eiusmodi: quae si verba ipsa spectes, ad vetus Testamentum pertinent: cum tamen sub illo velo nobis Apostolus ea proponat, quae ad nouum Testamentum referuntur. Quae si Potificios non mouent: saltem ipsi se audiant, qui hunc Dauidicu uersum identide in suis templis repetunt.
units.tr: All the sheep of Kedar shall be gathered to you, he says; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you; they shall come up on my altar with favour, and I will adorn the house of my majesty. So too John made mention of the heavenly altar, the censer, the incense, the temple, the outer court, and the ark of the covenant itself and other such things, which if you look at the words themselves belong to the Old Testament; yet under that veil the Apostle sets before us things that refer to the New Testament. If these things do not move the Papists, at least let them hear themselves, who repeat this verse of David in their own temples:

units.la: Tunc acceptabis sacrificiu iustitia, oblationes & holocausta: tunc imponent super altare tuum vitulos: Quę verba, ut nostris temporibus accommodentur, esse de spiritualibus, non aute externis sacrificiis intelligenda, credo, non negabunt. Nisi forte, vitulorum nomine, suos sacrificulos intelligant, ad sua illa altaria mugientes, & Euangelicae veritati, quantum in ipsis est, obstrepentes.
units.tr: Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings; then they will place calves upon your altar. I do not think they will deny that these words, if they are to be applied to our times, must be understood of spiritual, not external, sacrifices. Unless perhaps by calves they mean their own little sacrificers, lowing at their altars and clamouring against evangelical truth, so far as lies in them.

units.la: Obiectio 12.
units.tr: Objection 12.

units.la: A tempore quum ablatum, uerit inge sacri- Daniel.12. ficium & posita fuerit abominatio in desolatione, dies mille, ducenti, nonaginta, inquit Daniel: Ergo Missa sacrificium legitimum est.
units.tr: From the time that the continual sacrifice is taken away and the abomination is set up in the desolation, there shall be a thousand two hundred and ninety days, says Daniel (Daniel 12). Therefore the Mass is a lawful sacrifice.

units.la: Consequentia patet. Nam hic locus intelligendus est de fine mundi, ut perspicuum est ex antecedentibus, ubi loquitur Daniel de mortuorum resurrectione. Illis igitur novissimis temporibus erit iuge sacrificium auferendum, Antichristo saeviente. Quod quidem sacrificium Missam significat. Nam spiritualia sacrificia Christianorum multa sunt & multiplicia. Hoc autem sacrificium est iuge: hoc est idem, simplex eodemque modo saepius repetendum.
units.tr: The inference is clear. For this passage must be understood of the end of the world, as is plain from what goes before, where Daniel speaks of the resurrection of the dead. In those last times, then, the continual sacrifice will be taken away, while Antichrist rages. And this sacrifice signifies the Mass. For the spiritual sacrifices of Christians are many and various. But this sacrifice is continual: that is, it is one and the same, simple, and to be repeated often in the same way.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Ridicula est Consequentia, cuius praecipuos aliquot errores recensebimus.
units.tr: The inference is ridiculous, and I shall point out some of its chief errors.

units.la: Primus error. Quod ea quae dicuntur de iugi sacrificio auferendo, praecise restringuntur ad tempora Antichristi. Nam in cap. 11. Daniel fecit mentionem iugis sacrificij tollendi, & ponendae abominationis, iisdem prorsus vocabulis vsurpatis, quibus vtitur in hoc cap. 12. de quo disputamus. At illum locum plerique de Antiocho exponunt: alij, vt ex Pontificiis permulti, referunt ad vltimum excidium vrbis Hierosolymae. Cur ergo non patiemur, locum hunc cap. 12. nos de vltimo etiam illo excidio intelligere? Atenim, inquis, pauo ante meminit resurrectionis mortuorum, semper dicto cap. 12. ver. 2. Recte sane: & hoc ipsum argumentum premo: nedum me à sententia dimoueat. Cùm enim illa abominatio desolationis fuerit ante diē nouissimū futura: sequitur necessariò, quod aitDaniel in hoc cap.12.ver.11.de abomina-tione desolationis, esse ad ea quæ antè dixe-rat, referendum: ita vt hìc tantum modò spa-tium temporis addatur. Quinetiam verbum præteriti temporis Husar, hoc est, sublatum fuit, quo Daniel in hoc loco vsus est, cùm in cap.11. futurum tempus vsurpauerit: nostrā hanc sententiam plane confirmat. Quid porrò respondsuri sunt Christo, locum hunc Danielis apud Matthæum citanti, his verbis? Quum videritis abominationem desolationis quæ dicta est à Daniele Propheta positam in loco san-cto (qui legit animaduertat) Tunc qui fuerint in Iudæa fugiant in montes &c. Ex quibus omnibus intelligi potest, nihil esse causæ quamobrem hæc Danielis Prophetia ad Antichristi tempora restringatur: cùm potius certis argumentis effici posse, Danielis verba proprie, & vt sonant, esse de iugi sacrificio legali accipienda: quod interruptum fuit Antiochi temporibus, & postea penitus sublatum, quum vrbs Hierosolyma ab Romanis euersa & excisa est. Hoc autem si per applicationem plerique Doctores extendunt ad Antichristi tempora: vt fateor id cum fructu fieri posse: ita pernego, ex hac applicatione, vel dogma aliquod fidei constituendum, vel, propriam significationem verborum Danielis peruertendam esse.
units.tr: The first error is that what is said about the taking away of the continual sacrifice is strictly limited to the times of Antichrist. For in chapter 11 Daniel also mentions the taking away of the continual sacrifice and the setting up of the abomination, using exactly the same words that he uses in this chapter 12, which we are discussing. Yet most people explain that passage of Antiochus, and others, including many of the Papists, refer it to the final destruction of the city of Jerusalem. Why, then, should we not allow that this passage in chapter 12 also refers to that final destruction? But, you will say, a little before, he mentions the resurrection of the dead, in the same chapter 12, verse 2. Quite right, and I press this very argument, which does not move me from my view at all. For since that abomination of desolation is to come before the last day, it necessarily follows that what Daniel says in this chapter 12, verse 11, about the abomination of desolation must be referred to what he had said before, so that here only a span of time is added. Indeed, the past tense verb Husar, that is, "was taken away," which Daniel uses in this place, while in chapter 11 he used the future tense, plainly confirms our view. What, moreover, will they answer to Christ, who cites this passage of Daniel in Matthew with these words: When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, and so on? From all this it can be understood that there is no reason why this prophecy of Daniel should be restricted to the times of Antichrist. Rather, by sure arguments it can be shown that the words of Daniel are to be taken properly, and as they sound, of the continual legal sacrifice, which was interrupted in the times of Antiochus and afterwards utterly abolished when the city of Jerusalem was overthrown and destroyed by the Romans. If, however, many teachers extend this by application to the times of Antichrist, I admit that this can be done with profit; but I deny absolutely that from this application any doctrine of faith may be established, or the proper meaning of Daniel's words be perverted.

units.la: Secundus error παρὰ τὸ ἐνσόμενον. Fac enim Antichristi temporibus sublatum iri iuge sacrificium (vt vis) Ecquid hoc ad Missę sacrificium? Proferant locum Pontificij, ex quo bellam hanc suam interpretationem, aliqua saltem verisimilitudine confirmient. Re deamus igitur ad superiorem refutationem, quam ante iam aliquoties adhibuimus: ac Pontificios rogemus, an velint vocabulum Thamid, hoc est, iugiter (quod de iugi sacrificio plerique intelligunt: alij latius, de toto legali cultu exponunt) esse à Daniele in propria significatione vsurpatum, nec ne? Si illud malint: Missa igitur erit Iudaicum sacrificium. Si nolint: cur igitur yrget propriam significationem sacrificij, cum ne ipsum quidem sacrificij vocabulum extet in hac Danielis Prophetia? Patiantur sane, si iuge sacrificium metaphoricè vsurpatum sit: id nos de illo sacrificio intelligere, quod Ecclesiæ Christianæ temporibus conuenire, ex Apostolica doctrina didicimus. Quid igitur mirum si, Antichristo sæuiente, publicus Dei cultus ex ipsius verbo præscriptus, & exterior verę religionis professio ac forma sublata fuit? Quinetiam ex hac applicatione ad Antichristum, labefactatur aliud commentum Pontificiorum de visibili Ecclesię successione nunquam interrumpenda, qua de re nos alibi disputaui-mus. mus. At, inquiunt, sacrificia Christianorum spiritualia, sunt multiplicia. Iuge autem sacrificium, vnū & simplex esse oportet. Ego vero potius audio Paulū affirmantem vnam esse fidem & vnū Baptisma. Atque inde colligo in Ecclesia Christiana vnā esse veritatē, ac propterea vnius veritatis vnam esse exteriorem profesionem. Habeant ergo Pōtificij illam multiplicitatē: quorum fides humanis statutis, iisdémque variis ac multiplicibus, non autē vno Dei verbo nititur. Quāquam, quid sibi volunt, quū Missæ sacrificiū simplex esse dicunt? Quid enim vnquam tā varium, multiplex & multiforme afferri possit? Nam vt taceam de Græcorū & Armenorum Missis, nec proferam multiplices, tum Episcoporum, tum Cardinaliū cęremonias, si quando forte dignantur ad sua altaria accedere: affirmo, nullā esse, ne minutulorum quidem Monachorum sectam, quæ non peculiarem aliquem ritum feruet in suo Missæ sacrificio faciendo. Etenim (vt sexcenta alia praetermittam) hic musitando, ille voce altiori Missam exorditur: alius stans, alius vero pronus, alius denique totus ad terram abiectus prostratúsq; (iuxta illud poëtæ: Procumbit humi bos) ad altare accedit. Quid porrò commemorem Missas de sanctis (quarum vnaquæque suam habet verborum conceptā formulā) Missas pro defunctis & innumerabilia eiusmodi Pontif. somnia, quibus scilicet suæ Missæ simplicitatem nobis hactenus cō mendarunt.Hæc igitur Pontificiorum obiectio quanti sit ponderis spero satis esse manifestum.
units.tr: The second error is a fallacy of the consequent [παρὰ τὸ ἐνσόμενον]. Grant that the continual sacrifice will be taken away in the times of Antichrist, as you wish. What has this to do with the sacrifice of the Mass? Let the Papists produce a passage from which they might at least confirm this bold interpretation of theirs with some plausibility. Let us therefore return to the refutation above, which we have already used several times, and ask the Papists whether they wish the word tamid, that is, "continually" (which most understand of the continual sacrifice, and others explain more broadly, of the whole legal worship), to have been used by Daniel in its proper sense or not. If they prefer that, then the Mass will be a Jewish sacrifice. If they do not, why do they insist on the proper sense of "sacrifice," when the very word "sacrifice" does not even occur in this prophecy of Daniel? Let them allow, certainly, that if the continual sacrifice is used metaphorically, we understand it of that sacrifice which we have learned from apostolic doctrine to be fitting for the times of the Christian Church. Why then is it surprising that, while Antichrist rages, the public worship of God prescribed by his own Word, and the outward profession and form of true religion, were taken away? Moreover, by this application to Antichrist, another invention of the Papists is undermined, that of a visible succession of the Church that is never to be interrupted; on this matter we have argued elsewhere. But, they say, the spiritual sacrifices of Christians are many and various, whereas the continual sacrifice ought to be one and simple. I, however, rather hear Paul affirming that there is one faith and one baptism. From this I gather that in the Christian Church there is one truth, and therefore one outward profession of the one truth. Let the Papists, then, have that manifoldness, since their faith rests on human statutes, which are themselves various and manifold, and not on the one Word of God. Yet what do they mean when they call the sacrifice of the Mass simple? For what has ever been produced that is so varied, manifold and multiform? For to say nothing of the Masses of the Greeks and Armenians, and not to mention the manifold ceremonies of bishops and cardinals, if they ever deign to approach their altars, I affirm that there is no sect even of the smallest monks that does not observe some peculiar rite in performing its sacrifice of the Mass. For (to pass over six hundred other examples) one begins the Mass in a murmur, another in a louder voice; one approaches the altar standing, another prone, and another finally, wholly cast down and prostrate on the ground (as the poet says: "the ox sinks to the ground"). Why should I mention further the Masses of the saints, each of which has its own form of words, the Masses for the dead, and countless other such dreams of the Papists, by which they have hitherto praised to us the simplicity of their Mass? The weight of this Papist objection, therefore, I hope is now sufficiently plain.

units.la: Superest vt incommodis propositis hunc errorem magis,magísque refellamus: ac primum id audiamus quod isti maximum incommodum esse ducerent.
units.tr: It remains to refute this error more and more by the inconveniences they propose, and first to hear what they would consider the greatest inconvenience.

units.la: Si inge sacrificium de quo Daniel locutus est, de sacrificio Missa intelligendum est: Ergo, vnicam in toto terrarum orbe Missam celebrari oporteret & in vno tantum loco, & bis in die: manè videlicet & vesperi: atque ita vespertina Pontificiorum cantiones in Missam conuerterentur: quod illi non ἀδωάτῳ modò sed etiam flagitium existimarent. Consequentia patet: quandoquidem ea fuit olim ratio iugis sacrificij, vt videre licet Exod.29. 1.Chro.16 &c. Item.
units.tr: If the continual sacrifice of which Daniel speaks must be understood of the sacrifice of the Mass, then the Mass would have to be celebrated only once in the whole world, and in only one place, and twice a day, namely in the morning and in the evening; and thus the Papists' evening chants would be turned into the Mass. They would think this not merely absurd but a disgrace [ἀδωάτῳ]. The inference is clear, since this was formerly the rule of the continual sacrifice, as may be seen in Exodus 29, 1 Chronicles 16, and so on. Likewise:

units.la: Si locus Danielis præcisè de Antichristo intelligendus est, & dierum numerus tres annos & sex menses significat: quibus exactis, & interimendus sit Antichristus, & futura mortuorum resurrectio, vt Pontificij tradunt: Ergo poterit præscirì non solum, tempus, verum etiam dies ipse nouissimi aduentus Christi. Ἀδωάτῳ, ex his Christi verbis, De die illo & hora nemo scit. Qua de re plura diximus alibi quum de vera Ecclesiæ successione ageremus.
units.tr: If the passage of Daniel must be understood strictly of Antichrist, and the number of days signifies three years and six months, after which Antichrist is to be destroyed and the resurrection of the dead is to follow, as the Papists teach, then not only the time but also the very day of the last coming of Christ can be known. [This is] absurd [ἀδωάτῳ], in view of Christ's words: Of that day and hour no one knows. We have said more about this elsewhere, when we treated of the true succession of the Church.

units.la: Vt igitur istum errorem corrigamus, ita statuendum est.
units.tr: So, to correct this error, the following must be established.

units.la: Quandoquidem eam Danielis Prophetiam, quam nobis obiiciunt Pontifici, constat esse perdifficile: idque vel ex ipso Daniele, cuius haec verba sunt, Audivi, inquit, sed non intellexi: aequum est, nos in eius interpretatione, magna cum reuerentia versari: diligenterque cauere, ne temere eam tractantes, aliquid inde colligamus, quod aliis Scripturae locis planis ac dilucidis repugnet. Cum igitur Daniel de futuris Ecclesiae persecutionibus, iisdemq; longe grauissimis prophetarit: quaenam illae, vel iam praeterierint, vel adhuc futurae sint, nec curiose quaerendum, nec temere definiendum est: Sed ea demum sunt affirmanda, quae cum expresis Scripturae testimoniis coueniunt. Praeclare enim Augustinus, quum hunc Danielis locum in manibus haberet, & de nouissimo Christi aduentu dissereret: Mihi quisquam non videtur errare, inquit, quum aliquid nescire se scit; sed, quum se putat scire, quod nescit.
units.tr: Since the prophecy of Daniel, which the Papists throw in our face, is admittedly very difficult, and this is plain from Daniel himself, whose words these are: I heard, he says, but I did not understand, it is fair that we deal with its interpretation with great reverence, and take care not to draw from it, when handling it rashly, anything that conflicts with other plain and clear passages of Scripture. Therefore, since Daniel prophesied of future persecutions of the Church, and those most grievous, it is neither to be inquired into curiously, nor to be defined rashly, which of those persecutions have already passed and which are still to come; rather, only those things are to be affirmed which agree with the express testimonies of Scripture. For Augustine rightly said, when he had this passage of Daniel in hand and was discussing the last coming of Christ: It seems to me that no one errs when he knows that he does not know something; but he errs when he thinks he knows what he does not know.

units.la: Obiectio 13.
units.tr: Objection 13.

units.la: Sacrificium Missae ipsis Apostolorum temporibus ab Ecclesia Christiana celebratum est: Est igitur legitimum.
units.tr: The sacrifice of the Mass was celebrated by the Christian Church in the very times of the Apostles. It is therefore lawful.

units.la: Antecedens probatur ex his locis.
units.tr: The antecedent is proved from these passages.

units.la: Obsecro primum omnium fieri obsecrationes, orationes, postulationes, gratiarum actiones pro omnibus hominibus, &c. ex Augustino.
units.tr: I urge, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions and thanksgivings be made for all men, etc. From Augustine.

units.la: Ministrantibus illis Domino & ieiunantibus. Græcè λειτυργούντων, hoc est, sacrificantibus.
units.tr: While they ministered to the Lord and fasted. In Greek [λειτυργούντων], that is, sacrificing.

units.la: Non potestis mensæ Domini participes esse & mensæ dæmoniorum. Mensam Domini intelligit altare, quia mensa dæmoniorum de altari intelligenda est.
units.tr: You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons. He means by "table of the Lord" the altar, because the "table of demons" must be understood of an altar.

units.la: Habemus altare de quo edere non habent potestatem qui tabernaculo deseruiunt. Si Christiani tum habebant altare, offerebant igitur sacrificium, nempe Missæ.
units.tr: We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat. If Christians then had an altar, they therefore offered a sacrifice, namely of the Mass.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Falsissimum est Antecedens. Error: Ψευδογραφημα in Theologia, vt erit perspicuum, postquam quatuor locos nobis obiectos excusserimus.
units.tr: The antecedent is utterly false. It is an error [ψευδογράφημα] in theology, as will be clear once we have examined the four passages put forward against us.

units.la: Primus locus ad rem non facit: Augustinus quidem Pauli verba ad Cœnæ Domini celebrationem accommodat: sed præterquam quòd nondum hîc agimus de argumentis ex veteribus petitis, locus Pauli, ipso etiam Augustino interprete, plane tollit externum Missæ sacrificium: nedum illud stabiliat. Nam si nec obsecrationes, nec orationes, nec postulationes, nec gratiarum actiones, sunt externum sacrificium proprie dictum: sed illa omnia dicuntur sacrificia spiritualia Christianorum, de quibus alio in loco disseruimus: relinquitur, vt in Cœna Domini nullum sit externum sacrificium.
units.tr: The first passage does not bear on the matter. Augustine indeed applies Paul's words to the celebration of the Lord's Supper; but, apart from the fact that we are not yet dealing with arguments drawn from the ancient writers, Paul's passage, even on Augustine's own interpretation, plainly removes the external sacrifice of the Mass, let alone establishes it. For if neither supplications, nor prayers, nor petitions, nor thanksgivings are the external sacrifice properly so called, but all these are called the spiritual sacrifices of Christians, of which we have treated elsewhere, then it follows that in the Lord's Supper there is no external sacrifice at all.

units.la: Secundus locus depravatus est. Error est παρα
units.tr: The second passage is corrupted. The error is [παρὰ]

units.la: παρὰ τὸ χῆμα τῆς λέξεως. Nam λειτυργεῖν est publico fungi munere: ac proinde ex loci circunstantia exponendum est: significat autem apud Lucam publicè docere: quandoquidem ibi agitur de publicis Ecclesiæ doctoribus: Fateor quidem ipsam Euangelij prædicationem aliquando sacrificium dici per simi​litudinem, propter eas rationes quæ à nobis alibi commemoratæ sunt (sic enim Paulus meminit oblationis Gentium & λειτυργίας fidei, seq; adeò vocat Christi λειτυργὸν, apud Getes ἱερυργοῦντα τὸ εὐαγγέλιον) sed quàm hoc sit alienum ab externo Missæ sacrificio, vel ipsi Pontificij satis vident. Cur autem ieiunium tribuant iis qui Missæ sacrificium faciunt, non intelligo: cum ad illud suum altare, coram aliis ieiunis, illi soli manducent ac bibant.
units.tr: [παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τῆς λέξεως], a mistake against the figure of the word. For [λειτουργεῖν] means to discharge a public office; accordingly it must be explained from the context of the passage, and in Luke it means to teach publicly, since there the public teachers of the Church are in question. I admit indeed that the very preaching of the gospel is sometimes called a sacrifice by way of likeness, for the reasons we have mentioned elsewhere (for Paul too speaks of the offering of the Gentiles and of the [λειτουργία] of faith, and calls Christ the [λειτουργὸς], and among the Greeks the gospel is said to be [ἱερουργοῦντα] the gospel). But how far this is from the external sacrifice of the Mass even the Papists themselves see well enough. Why they assign fasting to those who make the sacrifice of the Mass, I do not understand, since it is those alone who eat and drink at their altar while others fast.

units.la: Tertius locus corruptus est errore consimili. Est enim ridiculum nomine mensæ, altare intelligi ab Apostolo, cuius isti nec verba nec sententiam tenent. Nam ibi Paulus non agit de Ethnicorum altaribus, sed de eorum conuiuiis in honorem idolorum celebratis; quibus Christianos interesse vetat: quippe ipsius idololatriæ appendicibus. Itaque cum poculi meminisset, statim addidit mensam, exegeticè, vt se de ipsis Ethnicorum conuiuiis loqui testaretur. Ageba tur enim de esu idolothytorum, hoc est eorum quæ erat idolis, nō sacrificāda, sed sacrificata.
units.tr: The third passage is corrupted by a similar error. For it is ridiculous that the Apostle should be understood to mean an altar by the name of table, when these men hold neither his words nor his meaning. For Paul there is not dealing with the altars of the Gentiles, but with their feasts celebrated in honour of idols, to which he forbids Christians to come, since they are appendages of idolatry itself. So when he had mentioned the cup, he at once added "table", explaining it, to show that he was speaking of the feasts of the Gentiles themselves. For the question was about eating things offered to idols, that is, things which were not to be sacrificed to idols but already sacrificed.

units.la: Porrò vocabulum poculi expendendum est, Non potestis, inquit, poculum Domini bibere & poculum dæmoniorum. Ethnicos autem in suis altaribus bibisse,ne fando quidem audi tum est: hoc enim peractis sacrificiis facti-tabant.Vnde Athenæus, μεθύειν quasi μεῖλα τὸ θύειν dictum existimat: eò quòd postquâ sacrificauerant,solerent in solennibus illis conuiuiis ebrietati indulgere. Quid, quod isti nihil tale cogitantes, ipsi se refellunt? nam si mensa apud Paulum altare significat (vt volunt)& Paulus non ad solosPresbyte-ros scripsit,sed ad totam Corinthiorũ Ec-clesiam (vt manifestum est) sequetur totam Ecclesiam priscis illis temporibus Cœnæ Domini sub vtraque specie (vt vulgò dicūt) communicare solitam fuisse: & istud altare, pro quo tantopere decertant Pontificij,non fuisse Presbyterorum proprium. Bis autem ridiculum est,quod isti concludunt:Si men-sa dæmoniorum altare significet,inde sequi, per mensam Domini,altare esse intelligen-dum: quasi verò idem vocabulum variè ac-ceptum, non possit ad res diuersas signifi-candas adhiberi: vt vicisim res eadē variis nominibus significatur, alio atque alio re-spectu. Sic altare vocant Pontificij, quate-nus opinantur se sacrificium reale facere: quatenus autem sacrificulus illic comedit & bibit: certè hoc respectu, nō iā altare,sed mensam dicendā esse fateantur necesse est.
units.tr: Next, the word "cup" must be weighed. "You cannot," he says, "drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons." Now that the Gentiles drank at their altars is not even to be spoken of; for they made merry after the sacrifices were completed. Hence Athenaeus thinks [μεθύειν] (to be drunk) was so called as if [μετὰ τὸ θύειν] (after sacrificing), because after they had sacrificed they were accustomed to indulge in drunkenness at those solemn feasts. And what of the fact that these men, not thinking of any such thing, refute themselves? For if in Paul "table" signifies an altar (as they wish), and Paul wrote not only to the elders but to the whole Church of the Corinthians (as is manifest), it will follow that in those early times the whole Church was accustomed to communicate in the Lord's Supper under both kinds (as it is commonly said), and that that altar, for which the Papists contend so fiercely, was not the proper possession of the elders. It is doubly ridiculous, however, that they conclude thus: if the "table of demons" signifies an altar, it follows that by "table of the Lord" an altar must be understood; as if the same word, taken in different senses, could not be used to signify different things, just as, conversely, the same thing is signified by different names according to different points of view. So the Papists call it an altar in so far as they think they make a real sacrifice there; but in so far as their little priest eats and drinks there, they must surely admit that in that respect it ought to be called not an altar but a table.

units.la: In quarto loco similem errorem admit-tunt. Nam altaris vocabulum Apostolus nō vsurpat proprie, vt significat altare aspe&ta-bile & materiatum, sed, figuratè, pro ea re quam altare veteris Testamenti & omnes cæremoniæ legales adumbrarunt; nomén-que signi tribuit ipsi rei significatæ. Quis enim non facilè animaduertat, Apostolum altare illud opponere legali Tabernaculo: ac propterea altari materiato, quod erat in ipso Tabernaculo collocatū. Nam Iudæos obstinatè cæremoniis legalibus addi&tos,& Christū præfractè reiicientes, ab ipso Christo & ab eius meritis excludit. Quid, quod verum Tabernaculum legali adumbratum idem Apostolus manifestè dicit nō esse manufactum? quomodo igitur manufactum erit altare, quod etiam nomine Tabernaculi comprehenditur? Quid porrò dicturi sunt de altari illo cuius Ioannes mentionem sæpe facit in Apocalypsi? num crassa quædam & lapidea altaria nobis in cœlo fabricabunt? Desinat igitur Pontificij fallere παρὰ τῷ ἐμωνυμίαν. Atque ita existiment, nos repudiatis, non tantum legalibus, sed etiam Pontificiis altaribus, habere nostrum altare, nempe Christum Dominum nostrū in quo & per quem nostras preces, gratiarū actiones, nostra omnia, denique nos totos Deo offerimus. Sic enim Apostolus locum hunc de vero Christianorum altari concludens,
units.tr: In the fourth passage they make a similar error. For the Apostle does not use the word "altar" properly, to signify a visible and material altar, but figuratively, for that reality which the altar of the Old Testament and all the legal ceremonies foreshadowed; and he gives the name of the sign to the thing signified. For who does not readily perceive that the Apostle sets this altar against the legal tabernacle, and therefore against the material altar which stood in the tabernacle itself? For he shuts out from Christ and his merits the Jews, who were stubbornly bound to legal ceremonies and obstinately rejected Christ. Moreover, the same Apostle plainly says that the true tabernacle, of which the legal one was a shadow, is not made with hands; how then will the altar be made with hands, when it too is comprehended under the name of tabernacle? What, further, will they say of that altar of which John often makes mention in the Apocalypse? Will they build for us in heaven some gross altars of stone? Let the Papists therefore cease to deceive by equivocation [παρὰ τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν]. And let them consider that we, having rejected not only the legal altars but also the Papist altars, have our own altar, namely Christ our Lord, in whom and through whom we offer to God our prayers, thanksgivings, all that we have, and finally ourselves entirely. For the Apostle, concluding this passage about the true altar of Christians, says thus:

units.la: Per ipsum igitur, inquit, assidue offeramus Deo sacrificium laudis, id est, fructum labiorum confitentium nomini eius. En tibi altare, en sacrificia, quae nobis Apostolus commendauit. Sed praestat hoc argumentum Pontificiorum vno verbo in ipsos regerere.
units.tr: "Through him, therefore," he says, "let us continually offer to God the sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name." Behold your altar, behold the sacrifices which the Apostle commended to us. But it is better to turn this argument of the Papists back upon them in a single word.

units.la: Si ex visibili altari, sequitur, intelligendum esse visibile sacrificium (vt argumentantur Pontifici) Ergo simili ratione ex inuisibili sacrificio, sequitur, intelligendum esse altare inuisibile. Apostolus autem de Christianorum altari loquens non proponit externum aliquod sacrificium: sed inuisibile & spirituale tantum. Ex quo efficitur: Altare de quo locutus est, non crasse, sed spiritualiter intelligendum esse. Quae cum ita sint, merito negauimus quod a Pontificiis propositum fuit, Missae sacrificium ipsis Apostolorum temporibus ab Ecclesia Christiana celebratum fuisse.
units.tr: "If from a visible altar," they argue, "it follows that a visible sacrifice must be understood (as the Papists argue), then by a similar reasoning, from an invisible sacrifice it follows that an invisible altar must be understood. But the Apostle, speaking of the altar of Christians, does not propose any external sacrifice, but only an invisible and spiritual one. From which it follows that the altar of which he spoke must be understood not grossly but spiritually." Since these things are so, we rightly denied what the Papists put forward, that the sacrifice of the Mass was celebrated by the Christian Church in the very times of the Apostles.

units.la: Hactenus eas Pontificiorum obiectiones discussimus, quas illi sibi videbantur ex sacris literis depromere, vt suum Missae sacrificium externum & reale comprobarent. Sed quia, dum illis diffidunt, identidem se in veterum doctorum syluam coniiciunt, vt in eorum vmbra delitescant: age nos etiam audiamus isthaec eorum argumenta, vt dispiciamus quantum illa valere possint.
units.tr: Thus far we have examined those objections of the Papists which they seemed to draw from the holy writings, so as to establish their external and real sacrifice of the Mass. But because, while they distrust these, they repeatedly throw themselves into the forest of the ancient teachers, to hide in their shadow, come, let us also hear those arguments of theirs too, so that we may see how much they can avail.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: SIc igitur Pontificij veterum Doctorum sententias nobis opponunt.
units.tr: Thus the Papists set before us the opinions of the ancient teachers.

units.la: Obiectio 1.
units.tr: Objection 1.

units.la: Agnum Paschalem figuram fuisse sacrificij Missæ, veteres tradiderunt. Quare legitimum est Missæ sacrificium.
units.tr: That the Paschal lamb was a figure of the sacrifice of the Mass, the ancients have taught. Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass is lawful.

units.la: Antecedens patet ex Chrysost.serm. de prodit.Iud.& Homil.83. in Matth. Tertul.lib. 4. Contr. Mar.&c. Hier.lib.4.in cap. 26. Matt. &c.
units.tr: The antecedent is clear from Chrysostom, in his sermon on the betrayal of Judas, and in Homily 83 on Matthew; from Tertullian, book 4 Against Marcion, etc.; from Jerome, book 4 on Matthew chapter 26, etc.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Ex solo Dei verbo dogmata Christianæ religionis esse statuenda, probauimus certa hac de re à nobis instituta disputatione, quâ inscripsimus, De Verbo Dei scripto aduersus human. Traditiones: nec audiendos veteres censemus, nisi quatenus cum verbo Dei consentiunt. Quamobrem ea quæ sequuntur in eam partem accipi nolim, quasi censeam, hoc fidei caput de quo disputamus, esse veterum authoritate definiendum. Hoc enim nobis tantum propositum est, excutere, satis-ne rectè Pontificij nobis veterum sententias obiiciant: adeo vt deinceps, non tâ pro nobis, quàm pro ipsis veteribus disputare videamur, quos illi trahût in suorû errorû societate. Vt enim fateor veteres Doctores suos quoque naevos habuisse: ita vehementer nego, eos qui probatiores habentur, vnquam existimasse quod isti suis Decretis sanciuerunt; nempe Missam esse verum & externum sacrificium propitiatorium pro peccatis nostris. Iam igitur superiorem obiectionem attendamus.
units.tr: By a careful dispute of our own, entitled On the Written Word of God against Human Traditions, we have already shown that the doctrines of the Christian religion must be settled by the Word of God alone. We judge that the ancients are to be heard only so far as they agree with the Word of God. Therefore I would not have what follows taken in the sense that I think this article of faith, which we are discussing, is to be defined by the authority of the ancients. Our only purpose here is to examine whether the Papists rightly set the opinions of the ancients against us, so that from now on we seem to be arguing less for ourselves than for the ancients themselves, whom they draw into the fellowship of their errors. For although I admit that these ancient teachers had their blemishes too, I strongly deny that those who are held in highest esteem ever thought what these men have sanctioned by their decrees: namely, that the Mass is a true and external propitiatory sacrifice for our sins. Let us now therefore consider the earlier objection.

units.la: Falsum est tum Antecedens, tum Consequens. Dico falsum esse Consequens, eo quod nullum vnquam sacrificium legitimum humana authoritate constitutum fuit.
units.tr: Both the antecedent and the consequent are false. I say the consequent is false, because no lawful sacrifice has ever been established by human authority.

units.la: Falsum etiam Antecedens affirmo esse: duabus rationibus.
units.tr: I also affirm that the antecedent is false, for two reasons.

units.la: Prior est: quia veteres (qui modo nomen aliquod in Ecclesia obtinuerunt) nunquam accommodarunt Agnũ Paschalem ad Missas sacrificium: imo nunquam sacrifici Missae meminerunt. Sed Christum ipsum fuisse Agno Paschali figuratum docuerunt: adeo vt Christus passus (est enim vtendum Iere verbis) Pascha adimpleuerit. Saepe quidem Sacram Domini Coenam tractantes, ad Agnum Paschale alluserunt: sed valere consequens, à S. Coena Domini, ad Missas sacrificium, hoc vero constantissime pernegamus. Error est παρα τῷ ἀγνοῶν ἐλέγχω.
units.tr: The first is this: the ancients (at least those who have gained any name in the Church) never applied the Paschal lamb to the sacrifice of the Mass; indeed they never mentioned the sacrifice of the Mass at all. But they taught that Christ himself was prefigured by the Paschal lamb, so that Christ, suffering (for I must use Jerome's words), fulfilled the Passover. Often, when treating of the Lord's Supper, they did allude to the Paschal lamb; but that it follows from the Lord's Supper to the sacrifice of the Mass, we most firmly deny. This is an error convicted by ignorance [παρὰ τῷ ἀγνοῶν ἐλέγχω].

units.la: Posterior ratio: quia veteres, si quando Agnum Paschalem accommodarunt Coenae Domini, similitudinem inter Agnum illum & S. Coenā constituerunt, in ipsa manducatione: qua Christum pro nobis cruci-fixum fixum participamus. Sic enim CHRYSO-STOMVS in eo loco quem nobis obijciunt, Ad mysteriorum, inquit, sacram celebrationem multos festinare inspicio: vt igitur, & cœlestis me-sa satietate perfruantur, & nostro sermone non ca-reant, tractatus congrue temperetur. Item, Nemo sit Iudas in mensa, hoc sacrificium, cibus spiritua-lis est. Et alio in loco ages de Cœna D. Chri-stus, inquit, hoc mysterium tradidit quando le-gem iam cessare oportebat. Praecipuam autem eorum solennitatem dissoluit [nempe Agni Paschalis] ac ad aliam tremendam mensam eos co-uocans dicit: Accipite, comedite, hoc est corpus meum. Idem alibi, Pascha Iudai celebrabant, ita vt in speculo & ænigmate: ineffabilia autem mysteriu non intellexerunt quæ illis rebus adum-brabantur: Quod filius Dei carnem induitus ma-standus esset & orbem terrarum vniuersum libe-raturus: Graecis, Barbaris, sanguinem gustandum exhibiturus, cœlum omnibus aperturus, quæ istic bona sunt humano generi communicaturus: car-nem hanc mastatam sumens supra cœlum sublatu-rus, & ad dextram Patris collocaturus esset. Hæc Chrysostomus de Agni Paschalis veri-tate disserens, & nihil nobis de Missæ sacri-ficio proponens.
units.tr: The second reason is this: when the ancients did apply the Paschal lamb to the Lord's Supper, they drew the likeness between that lamb and the Supper in the very eating, by which we partake of Christ crucified for us. For so Chrysostom, in the passage they cite, Ad mysteriorum, says: I see many hastening to the sacred celebration of the mysteries, so that they may enjoy the satiety of the heavenly table, and not be lacking in our sermon, and the discourse be suitably tempered. Likewise: Let no one be a Judas at the table; this sacrifice is spiritual food. And in another place: Christ, when the law ought already to have ceased, handed down this mystery at the Supper of the Lord. He dissolved their principal solemnity [namely, of the Paschal lamb] and, calling them to another tremendous table, says: Take, eat, this is my body. Likewise elsewhere: The Jews celebrated the Passover, as in a mirror and in a riddle; but they did not understand the unspeakable mysteries which were shadowed by those things: that the Son of God would put on flesh and be slain, and would set free the whole world; that he would give his blood to be tasted by Greeks and barbarians, would open heaven to all, and would share with the human race all the good things that are there; that, taking this slaughtered flesh, he would lift it above heaven and place it at the right hand of the Father. Thus Chrysostom, discoursing on the truth of the Paschal lamb, and setting before us nothing about the sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: TERTVLLIANVS quem obiiciunt: Professus, inquit, Christus, se concupiuisse edere Pascha vt suum (indignum enim vt quid alie-num concupisceret Deus) acceptum panem & distributum Discipulis corpus suum illum fecit,
units.tr: Tertullian, whom they cite: Christ, having professed that he desired to eat the Passover as his own (for it would be unworthy for God to desire what belongs to another), took bread and distributed it to the disciples, and made that his body,

units.la: L Hoc est corpus meum, dicendo: id est, figura corporis mei. Audiant Potitij & sentiant quàm infeliciter locum hunc citarint: atque hæc præsertim verba diligenter expendant: acceptum panem & distributum Discipulis.
units.tr: by saying "This is my body": that is, the figure of my body. Let the Papists hear, and perceive how unhappily they have cited this passage; and let them weigh especially these words: taking bread and distributing it to the disciples.

units.la: HIERONYMVS in loco nobis obiecto, In Luca legimus duos calices, inquit, vnum primi mensis, & alterum, secundi: vt qui inter sanctos primo mense Agnum comedere nō potuerit, secundo mense inter pœnitentes Agnum comedat. Idem: Pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus: si tamen comedamus illud in azymis sinceritatis & veritatis. Audiamus etiam quidnam alij ex veteribus hac de re censuerint.
units.tr: Jerome, in the passage they cite: In Luke we read of two cups, one of the first month and the other of the second; so that he who could not eat the Lamb among the saints in the first month, may eat the Lamb among the penitents in the second month. Likewise: Christ our Passover is sacrificed; let us therefore eat it in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Let us also hear what others among the ancients have judged in this matter.

units.la: Sic igitur BASILIVS. Celebremus Pascha, inquit, non in fermento malitiæ & nequitiæ: sed in azymis sinceritatis & veritatis: Immolata ad vesperum, hoc est, in consummatione seculi, vera illa one, nepe, Christo, cuius caro verus est cibus, &c.
units.tr: Thus Basil: Let us celebrate the Passover not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth: sacrificed at evening, that is, at the end of the age, that true Lamb, namely Christ, whose flesh is the true food, etc.

units.la: AVGVSTINVS. Pascha Iudæorum non nisi circuncisis dabatur. Purgatis enim solis & lauacro indulgentiæ cœlestis expiatis, percipiedi Christi corporis, sacrati cibi, facultas porrigitur.
units.tr: Augustine: The Passover of the Jews was given only to the circumcised. For only when they had been cleansed and atoned for by the washing of heavenly indulgence was the opportunity offered to receive the body of Christ, the consecrated food.

units.la: AMBROSIVS. Sumamus feruenti spiritu sacramentum in azymis sinceritatis & veritatis: atque eiusmodi pleraque. Et, ne scholasticos plane negligere videamur: Sic Thomas locum In 1. Cor. cap. 5. Apostoli tractas: Quia Christus immolatus est, Pascha nostru, inquit, Itaque epulemur: scilicet, manducantes Christum, nō solum sacramentaliter (secun(secundum illud Ioan. 6. Nisi manducaueritis carnem filij hominis, & biberitis eius sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis) sed spiritualiter, fruendo sapientia eius. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum esse poterit, quatenus & quo sensu, veteres Agnum Paschalem ad S. Domini Coenam accommodarint.
units.tr: Ambrose: Let us receive with fervent spirit the sacrament in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; and many things of this kind. And lest we seem to neglect the schoolmen altogether: Thomas, expounding the apostle's passage in 1 Corinthians chapter 5, says: "Because Christ was sacrificed, our Passover, therefore let us feast": namely, by eating Christ, not only sacramentally (according to John 6: "Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have no life in you"), but spiritually, by enjoying his wisdom. From all these things it will be clear in what way, and in what sense, the ancients applied the Paschal lamb to the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Obiectio 1.
units.tr: Objection 1.

units.la: Missa sacrificium fuisse oblatione Melchisedeci figuratum veteres tradiderunt. Quare, legitimum est Missae sacrificium.
units.tr: The Fathers handed down that the Mass was a sacrifice prefigured by the offering of Melchizedek. Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass is lawful.

units.la: Antecedens patet ex Augusti lib. 17. De Ciui. D. cap. 17. l. 1. Contr. aduersus leg. & Prophet. cap. 20. Hieronymus in Epist. ad Euagr. Ambr. lib. 5. de Sacram. Cypr. lib. 3. Epist. 2. &c.
units.tr: The antecedent is plain from Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 17, chapter 17; Contra adversarios legis et prophetarum, book 1, chapter 20; Jerome, in his letter to Evagrius; Ambrose, De Sacramentis, book 5; Cyprian, Epistle 2, book 3; etc.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Ne mihi repetenda sit ratio cur istud Consequens falsum sit (eam enim propositui in responsione ad superiorem proximam obiectionem) Antecedens excutio: atque id falsum esse duabus itidem rationibus demonstro.
units.tr: I need not repeat the reason why that consequent is false, since I set it out in my answer to the previous objection. I examine the antecedent instead, and I show by two reasons that it is false.

units.la: Prior ratio: quia (vt in superiori responsio ne diximus) veteres illi quos nobis obiiciunt, non locuti sunt de Missa: sed de Coena D. sacram: quod nihil habet cum Missa commune, nisi lucem cum tenebris simul coniunxeris.
