units.tr: The first reason: as we said in the earlier answer, those ancient writers whom they cite did not speak of the Mass but of the holy Supper of the Lord. That has nothing in common with the Mass, unless you join light with darkness.

units.la: Posterior ratio: quia veteres dum ad Eucharistiam referunt panem & vinum quae Melchisedecus protulit, non eo spectant, vt inde sacrificium aliquod externum & reale constituat, in quo Christus denuo offeratur: imo (si paucos excipias) non existimarunt Melchi-sedecum obtulisse Deo panem & vinum,sed hac ratione mysterium Eucharistiæ magis magisque commendare voluerūt: quòd iam priscis illis temporibus, iisdem signis, nem-pe pane & vino Abrahamo exhibitis, Chri-stus fuerit adumbratus, quæ quidem longè postea Christus ipse instituit in sacra Cœna, vt nos faceret sui corporis & sanguinis participes. Sed id Hieronymi verbis quàm meis explicare malo. Postquam, inquit, typicum Pascha fuerat impletum & Agni carnes cum Apostolis comederat: assumit panem qui confortat cor hominis, & ad verum Pascha transgreditur sacramentum, vt quomodo in præfiguratione eius, Melchisedec summi Dei sacerdos panē & vinum offerens fecerat, ipse quoque veritatem sui corporis & sanguinis repræsentaret. Atque id quod dicimus, loci contra nos citati plane confirmant.
units.tr: The second reason: when the ancients relate the bread and wine that Melchizedek brought forth to the Eucharist, they do not mean by this to establish from it some external and real sacrifice in which Christ is offered again. Rather, with few exceptions, they did not think Melchizedek offered bread and wine to God at all. They wished instead to commend more and more the mystery of the Eucharist, by this argument: that already in those early times Christ was foreshadowed by the same signs, bread and wine, which were set before Abraham, and which Christ himself long afterwards instituted in the holy Supper, to make us partakers of his body and blood. But I prefer to explain this in Jerome's words rather than my own. After, he says, the typical Passover had been fulfilled and he had eaten the flesh of the lamb with the apostles, he takes up the bread which strengthens the heart of man, and passes over to the true Passover sacrament, so that, just as Melchizedek, the priest of the most high God, offering bread and wine had done in the figure of it, he himself too might represent the truth of his body and blood. And what we say is plainly confirmed by the passages cited against us.

units.la: Vbique, inquit Avgvstinvs, offertur subsacerdote Christo quod protulit Melchisedec, quando benedixit Abraham. Audite Pontificij Pontificiæ Transsubstantiationis patroni: & iam vos pœniteat Augustinum huc vocasse. Et alibi dicit quidem tale sacrificium offerri: nimirum eo quòd panis & vinum in sacramento Cœnæ D.adhibentur.
units.tr: Everywhere, says Augustine, is offered, with Christ as subpriest, what Melchizedek brought forth when he blessed Abraham. Hear this, you Papists, you patrons of transubstantiation: and let it now grieve you that you summoned Augustine here. Elsewhere he indeed says that such a sacrifice is offered, namely because bread and wine are used in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Sic porrò Hieronymus nobis obiectus aliorum sententiam commemorans. Ordinem eius multis modis interpretantur, inquit, quit,quòd solus & Rex fuerit & sacerdos & ante Circuncisionem functus sacerdotio &c. neque carnis & sanguinis victimas immolauerit, sed pane & vino simplici puróque sacrificio, Christi dedicauerit sacramentum. Hæc Hieronymus ex aliorum sententia signorum similitudine consiederans: qui videntur exhibitionem panis & vini sacrificium appellare. Huc certè Thomas accedit ita locum hunc de Melchisedeco tractans. Sacerdos, inquit, debet exhibere confortationem: primo per bona monita: secundò per sacramentorum administrationem benedicendo. Unde, Et benedixit ei, Gen.14.
units.tr: Jerome, cited against us, speaks in the same way when he recalls the opinion of others: They interpret his order in many ways, he says, namely that he alone was both king and priest, and held the priesthood before circumcision, etc., and that he did not offer the victims of flesh and blood, but with bread and wine, a simple and pure sacrifice, he consecrated the sacrament of Christ. Jerome sets these things down from the opinion of others, reflecting on the likeness of the signs; they seem to call the offering of bread and wine a sacrifice. Certainly Thomas also comes close to this, treating this passage about Melchizedek in this way: A priest, he says, ought to give comfort: first by good admonitions, secondly by administering the sacraments through blessing. Hence, And he blessed him, Gen. 14.

units.la: AMBROSIVS autem: Quis, inquit, habuit panem & vinum? Melchisedec. Ipse ergo autor sacramentorum &c. Ergo primò intellige sacramenta hæc quæ accipis anteriora esse quàm sint Moysi sacramenta, &c. Idem: Cognouimus sacrorum istorum figurá Abrahæ temporibus præcessisse.
units.tr: Ambrose, however: Who, he says, had bread and wine? Melchizedek. He therefore was the author of the sacraments, etc. Therefore first understand that these sacraments which you receive are older than the sacraments of Moses, etc. The same: We have learned that the figure of these holy things came before the times of Abraham.

units.la: Denique CYPRIANVS: In sacerdote Melchisedec sacrificij Dominici sacramentum præfiguratum videmus. Et paulò pòst: Præcedit imago sacrificij Christi in pane & vino scilicet constituta. Loquitur autem de morte Christi: & hinc refellit Aquarios, qui sola aqua in Cœnę D. sacramento vtebantur: quòd Melchisedec vinum obtulerit. Ait autem Melchisedecum fuisse figuram Christi, qui Deo Patri suum corpus & sanguiné obtulit: quod Pontificij de suo incruento sacrificio intelligunt, cùm tamen Cyprianus de ipsa Christi morte & de sacrificio in cruce facto loquatur.Sic enim paulo post: Vt appareat, inquit, in Passione Dominica id esse gestum quod fuerat ante praedictum. Exponit locum Solomonis quem adiungit exemplo & figuras Melchisedeci tanquam de re vna eademq; intelligendum.Idé paulo ante de Noe dixit.Quod Noe typum futurae veritatis ostendens, non aquâ, sed vinum biberit & sic imaginem Dominicae Passionis expresserit. Haec ille.
units.tr: Lastly Cyprian: In the priest Melchizedek we see the sacrament of the Lord's sacrifice prefigured. And a little later: The image of Christ's sacrifice goes before, established, that is, in bread and wine. But he speaks of the death of Christ, and from this he refutes the Aquarians, who used only water in the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, because Melchizedek offered wine. He says, moreover, that Melchizedek was a figure of Christ, who offered his body and blood to God the Father; the Papists understand this of their own unbloody sacrifice, though Cyprian speaks of the very death of Christ and of the sacrifice made on the cross. For he says a little later: So that it may appear, he says, that in the Lord's Passion that was done which had been foretold before. He explains the passage of Solomon which he joins to the example and figure of Melchizedek, as if it were to be understood of one and the same thing. A little before this he said of Noah: Noah, showing the type of the future truth, drank not water but wine, and so expressed the image of the Lord's Passion. Thus far he.

units.la: Nihil igitur habet Pontificij in superioribus veterum Doctorum testimoniis, quo suae Missae sacrificium stabiliant. Etenim qui censent Eucharistiae mysterium fuisse adumbratum pane & vino, de quibus fit metio in Melchisedeci historia: Illi certe non propterea dicunt in Missa fieri verum, & externum sacrificium, in quo perepta panis & vini substantia Christus sacrificatur & offertur Deo. Imo potius ex superioribus veterum sententiis manifestum est, panem & vinum in Eucharistia remanere.
units.tr: Therefore the Papists have nothing in the testimonies of the ancient teachers cited above by which to establish the sacrifice of their Mass. For those who think the mystery of the Eucharist was foreshadowed by the bread and wine mentioned in the history of Melchizedek certainly do not on that account say that in the Mass there is a true and external sacrifice, in which the substance of bread and wine being destroyed, Christ is sacrificed and offered to God. Indeed, from the opinions of the ancients cited above it is plain rather that bread and wine remain in the Eucharist.

units.la: Quinetiam cum plerique veteres existimarint, Melchisedecum obtulisse Abrahamo panem & vinum: viderint Pontificij quam firmum argumentum ex hac veterum allegoria proferre possint.Sic enim Augustin. De Melchisedec loquitur, inquit, quia obviam Abrahae reverienti a caede regum & protulit panes & vinum, & obtulit ei & benedixit eum. Et AMBROSIVS. Tunc Abraham venit victor & occurrit illi Melchisedec sacerdos, & obtulit ei panem & vinum.
units.tr: Moreover, although most of the ancients thought that Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham, let the Papists see what a firm argument they can bring from this allegory of the ancients. For Augustine speaks thus of Melchizedek: Because he, says Augustine, brought out bread and wine to meet Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and offered them to him and blessed him. And Ambrose: Then Abraham came back victorious, and Melchizedek the priest went out to meet him, and offered him bread and wine.

units.la: Idem alibi, proponit sententiam Hebraeo- rum Doctorum: Quod Melchisedec in refe- rentione tam Abrahæ quàm pugnatorum eius, pa- nem vinumque protulerit, neque id Ambrosius repudiat. Tertul. Melchisedec Abra- hæ iam circuncifo reuertenti de prælio panem & vinum obtulit incircuncisus. Multa eiusmodi apud veteres occurrunt. Falluntur ergo Pontificij qui putant, veteres hunc typū in Melchisedeco commendare, quod is panem & vinum Deo obtulerit: illa enim prolata & oblata fuisse Abrahamo verbis dilucidis affirmant. Sed figuram illi constituunt in pane & vino: propterea quòd Christus illis ipsis signis adhibitis eos pascit suo corpore & sanguine, qui vera fide tantum beneficiū percipiunt. Atque ita volunt Melchisedecum fuisse typum Christi Ecclesiam pascentis suo corpore & sanguine. Ac ne à veterum campo (in quem sumus ingressi) recedamus, ecce tibi planis & perspicuis verbis apud Chrysostomum, quid veteres senserint de hac Melchisedeci figura. Sic enim ille, nobis explicans cur Abrahamus res oblatas à Sodomorum rege accipere recusarit: & panes ac vinum àMelchisedeco oblatum acceperit. A Melchisedec , inquit, non iniuria accepit: viri enim virtutem Divina Scriptura assignauit, dicens: Erat autem sacerdos Dei altissimi: quanuis aliâs quæ fiebant, Christi typus erant, & oblata, sacramentum quoddam præfignant: ideóque non renuit. Sic porrò Epiphanius aduersus Melchisedecianos: Quum Abraham fuit annorum 80. aut 90. plus minus, tunc Melchisedec ipsi obuiam venit, & propositit ipsi, panes & vinum, mysteriorum ænigmata præfigurans & exemplaria, cum Dominus nosier dicat, Ego sum panis viuens: & exemplar sanguinis ipsius, qui ex latere ipsius compuncto fluxit ad purgationem inquinatorum & resperionem ac salutem animarum nostrarum. Hæc ille. Ex quibus vides, hanc fuisse veterum sententiam, panem & vinum oblata, non Deo (nulli enim aut paucissimi ex veteribus vnquam ita locuti sunt) sed Abrahamo, fui isse exemplaria & typos Christi Domini nostri, qui sese in cruce pro nobis obtulit, & qui se nobis offert in Cœna vera fide recipiendū. Veteres igitur constituerunt similitudinem inter Melchisedecu offerente Abrahamo panem & vinum: & Christu offerentem seipsum nobis adhibitis panis & vini mysticis symbolis: tantum abest, ut de Christo Patri offerendo cogitarint. Eodem spectat hæc Chrysostomi verba: Quare dixit secundum ordinem Melchisedec? Et propter sacramenta, quod ille quoque panem & vinum Abraham obtulerit: & quod hoc sacerdotium sit à lege liberā, & quod neque finem, sicut dicit Paulus, nec principium habeat. Hæc Chrysostomus quæ extant etiam apud Basilium totidem verbis. Imò ipse Lombardus Scholasticorum pater: Huius sacramenti, inquit, ritum ostendit Melchisedec vbi panem & vinum Abrahæ obtulit. Damascenus autè: Pane & vino, inquit, excepit Melchisedec Abrahã : illa mensa hanc mysticam prÆsignauit. Hæc ille. Verùm: Quid vetat, inquis, panem & vinum ante oblata fuisse Deo, ac postea Abrahamo exhibita? Nimirū, quòd tuum sit somnium, non Scripturæ testimonium, in qua ne minimū quidem huiusce rei vestigium extat. Cæterùm non tantùm Melchisedeci panem & vinum allegoricè Veteres ad S. Cœnam retulerunt: sed etiam vinum quo Noachus inebriatus est: & hæc verba Iacobi Patriarchæ Gene.49. Lauabit in vino stolam suam. Vt videre licet apud Hieronymum & Cyprianum, ne mihi multa similia commemoranda sint. Quę quidem omnia satis magno argumento esse debent, quatenus ex veterum allegoriis liceat disputare. Quinetiam non desunt ex veteribus qui legalem & Aaronicam oblationem Similæ, censeant fuisse Eucharistiæ sacramentum: quod quàm alienū sit ab hac Melchisedeci allegoria, satis intelligunt ij qui tractatione Apostoli in Epi. ad Heb. attente perlegerunt.
units.tr: Elsewhere the same writer sets out the opinion of the Hebrew teachers: that Melchizedek, in refreshing both Abraham and his soldiers, brought forth bread and wine, and Ambrose does not reject this. Tertullian: Melchizedek, uncircumcised, offered bread and wine to Abraham, already circumcised, returning from battle. Many such things occur among the ancients. The Papists therefore are mistaken who think the ancients commend in Melchizedek a type of this, that he offered bread and wine to God; for they affirm in clear words that those things were brought forth and offered to Abraham. But they set up the figure in the bread and wine, for the reason that Christ, using those very signs, feeds with his body and blood those who receive the benefit only by true faith. And so they wish Melchizedek to have been a type of Christ feeding his Church with his body and blood. And, lest we leave the field of the ancients (into which we have entered), see here, in plain and clear words from Chrysostom, what the ancients thought of this figure of Melchizedek. For he, explaining to us why Abraham refused to accept the things offered by the king of Sodom, and accepted the bread and wine offered by Melchizedek, says: He did not accept [them] without reason, for Divine Scripture assigns to him the virtue of a man, saying: And he was priest of the most high God. Although the things that were done at that time were types of Christ, and the things offered foreshadow a certain sacrament; therefore he did not refuse. Epiphanius likewise, against the Melchizedeceans: When Abraham was about eighty or ninety years old, Melchizedek came to meet him, and set before him bread and wine, foreshadowing the enigmas and patterns of the mysteries, since our Lord says, I am the living bread; and the pattern of his blood, which flowed from his pierced side for the cleansing of the defiled and the sprinkling and salvation of our souls. Thus he. From these things you see that this was the opinion of the ancients: that the bread and wine were offered not to God (for none or very few of the ancients ever spoke so), but to Abraham, and were patterns and types of Christ our Lord, who offered himself on the cross for us, and who offers himself to us in the Supper to be received by true faith. The ancients therefore established a likeness between Melchizedek offering bread and wine to Abraham and Christ offering himself to us through the mystical symbols of bread and wine: so far were they from thinking of Christ being offered to the Father. To this same point belong these words of Chrysostom: Why does he say according to the order of Melchizedek? Because of the sacraments, namely that he too offered bread and wine to Abraham; and because this priesthood is free from the law, and has neither end nor beginning, as Paul says. Chrysostom says these things, which are also found in Basil in the same words. Indeed the Lombard himself, the father of the Scholastics: He shows, he says, the rite of this sacrament, where Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham. And Damascene: Melchizedek, he says, received Abraham with bread and wine; that table prefigured this mystical one. Thus he. But, you say, what forbids that the bread and wine were offered to God before and afterwards presented to Abraham? Surely this, that it is your dream and not a testimony of Scripture, in which not even the slightest trace of this thing is found. Moreover, the ancients related to the holy Supper not only the bread and wine of Melchizedek allegorically, but also the wine with which Noah was made drunk, and these words of the patriarch Jacob, Gen. 49: He will wash his garment in wine. As may be seen in Jerome and Cyprian, so that I need not recount many similar things. All these things should indeed be a sufficiently great argument, insofar as it is permitted to dispute from the allegories of the ancients. Nor are there lacking among the ancients those who think the legal and Aaronic offering of fine flour was the sacrament of the Eucharist; how far this is from this allegory of Melchizedek, those understand well enough who have read attentively the treatment of the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

units.la: Equidem (quod maiorum nostrorum pace dictum velim) tametsi non possum non laudare pium illud studium quo sacrū Cœnæ Dominicæ mysterium nobis commendare voluerunt: mallem tamen eiusmodi
units.tr: Indeed, with all due respect to our forefathers, though I cannot but praise the pious zeal with which they wished to commend to us the sacred mystery of the Lord's Supper, I would still have preferred that such allegories had been passed over.

units.la: Lib.4. Sent. d.8. Orthod. fid.l.4.c.14. Obiectio Pāt ifc.1. Resp.
units.tr: Lib. 4 Sent. d. 8. Orthod. fid. l. 4 c. 14. Objection of the Papists, ch. 1. Answer.

units.la: Ad Euagr. lib.2.Ep.3.
units.tr: To Evagrius, book 2, letter 3.

units.la: Iust.Mart. in Tryph. Ansatis conuenienter s eteres fa- stum Mel- chijedeci ad S.Cœnam re tulerint.
units.tr: The Fathers rightly referred the deed of Melchizedek to the Lord's Supper.

units.la: allegorias præterminissas.Atque adeo ab hac Melchisedeci,panem & vinum Abrahamo offerentis allegoria abstinere(meo quidem iudicio) præstitisset. Primum, quia nobis Sacramenta exhibentur in ipsa adhuc acie, hoc est, in hac vita, constitutis : neque tum exhibebūtur amplius, quum in vitam æter-nam recepti, deSatana,mundo,carne,deque omnibus viĉtis, prostratisque hostibus tri-umphum agemus. At Abrahamo Melchise-decus panem & vinum obtulit, non ad pu-gnam proficiscenti: sed à pugna reuerten-ti, & iam de fusis hostibus triumphanti. Deinde,nequid dissimulem, hæc allegoria videtur hausta ex fæce Rabbinica Iudæo-rum: ac propterea ab ipsis Christianis re-spuenda. Veteres enim Iudæi historiâ Mel-chisedeci allegoricè tractantes, existima-runt, ea fuisse significatum, tandem fore,vt sacrificia legalia Hierosolymæ fierent. Sed de his hactenus: nam superiori quidem ob-iectioni videtur à nobis satisfactum, ex iis quæ diximus.Quòd si nostra hac responsio-ne contenti non sint Pontificij : agè conuo-cemus ipsos Scholasticos & eos inter se co-mittamus,vt intelligant,etiam nobis tacen-tibus,suam sententiam corruere,à seipsa la-befactatâ.Sic igitur LOMBARDVS, quem illi Magistrum salutant.
units.tr: And so, in my judgment, it would have been better to abstain from this allegory of Melchizedek, who offered bread and wine to Abraham. First, because the sacraments are given to us while we are still in the battle line, that is, while we live in this life; and they will no longer be given when we are received into eternal life and, having struck down Satan, the world, the flesh, and all our conquered enemies, celebrate our triumph. But Melchizedek offered bread and wine to Abraham not as he set out to fight, but as he returned from battle and was already triumphing over the enemies he had routed. Next, lest I conceal anything, this allegory seems to have been drawn from the rabbinical dregs of the Jews, and for that reason it should be rejected by Christians themselves. For the ancient Jews, treating the history of Melchizedek allegorically, supposed that it signified that at last the legal sacrifices would be made at Jerusalem. But enough of these matters for now. For it seems we have satisfied the previous objection by what we have said. But if the Papists are not content with this our answer, let us summon the Scholastics themselves and set them against one another, so that they may understand that, even if we say nothing, their own opinion collapses, undermined by itself. Thus LOMBARD, whom they greet as their Master, says:

units.la: Presbyteri accipiunt calicē cum vino, & pa-tenam cum hostiis,vt per hoc sciant se accepisse potëpotestate placabiles Deo hostias offerendi: Hic ordo à filiis Aaron sumpsit initium. Hæc ille. Ex quibus nos ita concludimus.
units.tr: The presbyters receive the chalice with wine and the paten with the hosts, so that by this they may know that they have received the power of offering hosts that are placable to God. This order took its beginning from the sons of Aaron. So he. From these words we conclude as follows.

units.la: Si ordo Melchisedeci opponitur ordini Aaronis (ut docuit Apostolus) & Presbyterorum Pontificiorum ordo sumpsit initiu à filiis Aaronis (ut ille Magister affirmauit) & ipsum Missæ nomē deductū sit à vocabulo Missa in legalibus & Aaronicis cæremoniis vsurpato (quod quidā argutiores Monachi defendunt) Ergo nihil eorū quæ ab ipsis etiam Veteribus de sacerdotio Melchisedec dicta sunt, ad Presbyteros Pontificios, nec ad Missæ sacrificium pertinet.
units.tr: If the order of Melchizedek is set against the order of Aaron (as the Apostle taught), and the order of the Papistical presbyters took its beginning from the sons of Aaron (as that Master affirmed), and the very name of the Mass is derived from the word "Missa," used in the legal and Aaronic ceremonies (as some rather subtle monks defend), then nothing of what the Fathers themselves have said about the priesthood of Melchizedek pertains to the Papistical presbyters, nor to the sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: Obiectio 3.
units.tr: Objection 3.

units.la: Hanc Malachiæ Prophetiam: In omni loco sacrificatur & offertur nomini meo oblatio munda:Veteres de Missæ sacrificio expososuerūt. Quare: Missæ sacrificium est legitimum.
units.tr: The prophecy of Malachi: "In every place sacrifice is offered and a pure oblation to my name," the Fathers have expounded of the sacrifice of the Mass. Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass is lawful.

units.la: Antecedens patet ex Chrysost. Homil. in Psal. 95. Iren. lib. 4. c. 32. Iust. Mart. in Tryphone. August. de Ciuit. D. lib. 18. cap. 35. Eusebi, Cæsariensi. Demonst. Euan. lib. 1. cap. 10. Hieronymo in Malachiam. &c.
units.tr: The antecedent is evident from Chrysostom, Homily on Psalm 95; Irenaeus, book 4, ch. 32; Justin Martyr, in the Dialogue with Trypho; Augustine, De Civitate Dei, book 18, ch. 35; Eusebius of Caesarea, Demonstratio Evangelica, book 1, ch. 10; Jerome on Malachi; etc.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Answer.

units.la: Omnia vitiosa. Ac ne pluribus immoremur in refellendo consequenti: Fallit etiam Antecedens, eo modo quo superiora quæ iam redarguimus, Non enim veteres illi nobis obiecti, de Missa, sed de Cœnę Dominicæ sacramento locuti sunt. Cùm autē in S. Coena fieri,non reale & externum,vtPontifici] comminiscuntur,sed spirituale sacrificium veteres exiftimarint (qua de re postea nobis agendum erit) hinc factum est,vt oblationem de qua Prophetauit Malachias ad S.Coenam accommodarint. Errant igitur Pontificij suo more παρὰ τὸν ἀγγοιαν τῆς ἐλέγχος. Veteres autem locum Malachiae de spiritualibus Christianorum sacrificiis intelligere,ac propterea Pontificiorum sententiam euertere,nedum adiuuare, fiet ex ipsis eorum verbis manifestum.
units.tr: All of this is faulty. And, not to linger over many points in refuting the consequence: the antecedent also fails, in the same way as the earlier arguments we have already refuted. For those Fathers cited against us did not speak of the Mass but of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. Since they did not imagine, as the Papists do, a real and external sacrifice in the Supper, but held that the sacrifice there is spiritual (a matter we shall have to discuss later), it came about that they applied to the Supper the oblation of which Malachi prophesied. The Papists therefore err, as usual, [παρὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τῆς ἐλέγχου], through ignorance of the refutation. That the Fathers understood the passage of Malachi of the spiritual sacrifices of Christians, and therefore overturned rather than supported the Papistical opinion, will become plain from their own words.

units.la: CHRYSOSTOMVS quem nobis obiiciunt, postquam locum, Malachiae ad mysticam mensam(vt ille loquitur) hoc est,ad Coenae Dominicę sacramentū retulit:quod, veterum aliorum more sacrificium appellat(vt paulo post dicemus.) Est igitur,inquit, primum sacrificium quod ante dixi,spirituale illud ac mysticum donū de quo Paulus ait Eph. 5. Imitatores estote Dei tanquā filij dilecti & ambulate in dilectione quemadmodum & Christus dilexit nos, tradiditque seipsum pro nobis Deo sacrificium & oblationem in odorem suauitatis. Et aliquanto post, vocat sacrificium illud, salutare donum, nimirum quia in sacro illo mysterio Christū pro nobis passum ac mortuum vera fide recipimus. Idem Chrysostomus alio in loco tractans hanc Malachiae Prophetiam.Non per fumum ac nidorem, inquit,non per sanguinem ac redemptionis pretia sed sed per spiritus gratiam offertur.
units.tr: Chrysostom, whom they put forward against us, after referring the passage of Malachi to the mystical table (as he calls it), that is, to the sacrament of the Lord's Supper, calls it a sacrifice in the manner of other Fathers (as we shall say a little later). "Therefore," he says, "the first sacrifice, which I mentioned before, is that spiritual and mystical gift of which Paul says in Ephesians 5: 'Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma.'" And a little later he calls that sacrifice "a saving gift," namely because in that sacred mystery we receive with true faith Christ who suffered and died for us. The same Chrysostom, treating this prophecy of Malachi in another place, says: "It is not offered through smoke and a smell, nor through blood and the price of redemption, but through the grace of the Spirit."

units.la: IRENAEVS nobis obiectus verba Ma- lachię exponit deEucharistia, quatenus Deo gratias agimus pro summis eius in nos beneficiis. Atq; adeo tantum abest vt de Christo offerendo loquatur, vt potius de rerum creatarum oblatione verba faciat: ad vetustissimum illum Christianorum morem respiciens, quum illi Coenam Dominicam celebrantes, eleemosynas in pauperes conferrent: Christus, inquit, suis Discipulis dans consilium primitias Deo offerre ex suis creaturis: non quasi indigenti, sed vt ipsi nec infructuosi nec ingrati sint, eu qui ex creatura panis est accepit, &c. Noui Testamenti nouam docuit oblationem quam Ecclesia ab Apostolis accipiens in vniuerso mundo offert Deo, ei qui alimenta nobis praestat, primitias suorum munerum in nouo Testamento de quo Malachias praesignificauit, &c. Et paulo post. In omni loco incensum offertur nomini meo & sacrificium purum: incensa autem Ioannes in Apocalypsi orationes esse ait sanctorum. Idem postea: Quoniam igitur cum simplicitate Ecclesia offert, iuste munus eius purum sacrificium apud Deum deputatu est, quemadmodum & Paulus Philippensibus ait: Repletus sum acceptis ab Epaphrodito quae a vobis missa sunt, &c. oportet enim nos oblationem Deo facere & in omnibus gratos inueniri. Et aliquato post. Offerimus non quasi indigenti, sed gratias agentes donationi eius & sanctificantes creaturam: Quemadmodum enim Deus non indiget eorum quæ à nobis sunt: sic nos indigemus offerre aliquid Deo, sicut Salomon ait. Qui miseretur pauperis, fœneratur Deo. Qui enim nullius indigens est Deus, in se assumit bonas operationes nostras ad hoc ut præstet nobis retributionem bonorum suorum, sicut Dominus noster ait: Venite benedicti Patris mei, &c. esuriui enim & dedistis mihi manducare. Hæc ille. Porrò harum oblationum in celebratione Cœnæ Domini fieri solitarum meminit Ambrosius, inquiens. Quum una atque eadem prece omnium oblationes benedicerentur. &c. Non ausim tamen negare quin mos ille offerendarum eleemosynarum, publica prece adhibita, fuerit humanum additamentum, quo Veteres à priore Christi instituto iam deflectebant.
units.tr: Irenaeus, whom they put forward against us, expounds the words of Malachi of the Eucharist, insofar as we give thanks to God for his great benefits to us. And so far is he from speaking of offering Christ, that he rather treats of the offering of created things, looking to that most ancient custom of Christians, when at the celebration of the Lord's Supper they conferred alms upon the poor. "Christ," he says, "giving his disciples counsel to offer to God the firstfruits of his creatures: not as though he were in need, but that they themselves might be neither unfruitful nor ungrateful, he who has received bread from the creature, etc. He taught the new oblation of the New Testament, which the Church, receiving it from the Apostles, offers to God throughout the whole world, to him who provides us with food, the firstfruits of his gifts in the New Testament, of which Malachi prophesied beforehand, etc." And a little later: "In every place incense is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice; but John in the Apocalypse says that the incense is the prayers of the saints." Again afterward: "Since therefore the Church offers with simplicity, her gift is justly reckoned a pure sacrifice before God, just as Paul also says to the Philippians: 'I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things sent from you,' etc. For we must make an oblation to God and be found pleasing in all things." And a little after: "We offer not as though he were in need, but giving thanks for his gift and sanctifying the creature. For as God has no need of what is from us, so we need to offer something to God, as Solomon says: 'He who has pity on the poor lends to God.' For God, who lacks nothing, takes up our good works in himself, so that he may render to us the reward of his good things, as our Lord says: 'Come, blessed of my Father, etc., for I was hungry and you gave me food to eat.'" So he. Moreover, Ambrose mentions these offerings made at the celebration of the Lord's Supper, saying: "When the offerings of all were blessed by one and the same prayer, etc." Yet I would not dare to deny that the custom of offering alms, with a public prayer, was a human addition, by which the Fathers were already departing from Christ's earlier institution.

units.la: IVSTINVS MARTYR nobis obiectus vocat panem & vinum sacrificia, sed qualia sint hæc sacrificia ita exponit in illo ipso loco: Vt, inquit, gratias ageremus Deo, cum pro eo quod mundum cum universis quæ complectitur rebus, hominis gratia creavit: tum ob id etiam quod ab omni in qua fuimus malitia nos liberarit, ac principatus potestatésq; perfecta occiderit occidione per eum qui de consilio & voluntate eius factus est patibilis. hæc ille, ex quibus manifeste colligitur: S. Domini Cœnam à Iustino Martyre vocari sacrificium, videlicet Eucharisticum & gratiarum actionis, ac proinde spirituale.
units.tr: Justin Martyr, whom they put forward against us, calls bread and wine sacrifices, but in that same passage he explains what kind of sacrifices these are: "that we may give thanks to God, both because he created the world with all the things it contains for the sake of man, and also because he freed us from all the wickedness in which we were, and completely destroyed the principalities and powers by him who was made passible according to his counsel and will." So he. From which it is clearly gathered that the Supper of the Lord is called by Justin Martyr a sacrifice, namely a eucharistic sacrifice of thanksgiving, and therefore a spiritual one.

units.la: AVGVSTINVS quidem ait sacrificium offerri iuxta Prophetiam Malachiæ: nempe de Coenæ Dominicæ sacramento locum illum intelligens. Eiusmodi autem sacrificium esse spirituale, hoc est, sacrificium laudis, perspicuum est ex alio loco apud eundem Augustinum: Ecclesia, inquit, immolat Deo in corpore Christi sacrificium laudis ex quo Deus Deorum locutus vocauit terram à Solis ortu vsque ad Occasum: Hæc quippe Ecclesia, est Israel secundum spiritum, à quo distinguitur ille Israel secundum carnem, qui seruiebat in umbris sacrificiorum, quibus significabatur singulare sacrificium quod nunc offert Israel secundum spiritum, cui dictum est: Audi populus meus, &c. De huius enim domo non accipit vitulos. Iste immolat Deo sacrificiu laudis, &c. Et paulo post: In omni loco incensum offertur nomini meo, &c. Malach. 1. Incensum enim quod est Græce Thymiama, sicut exponit Ioannes in Apocalypsi orationes sunt sanctorum.
units.tr: Augustine indeed says that a sacrifice is offered according to the prophecy of Malachi, understanding that passage of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper. That such a sacrifice is spiritual, that is, a sacrifice of praise, is plain from another passage of the same Augustine: "The Church," he says, "offers to God in the body of Christ the sacrifice of praise, of which God, speaking as the God of gods, called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. For this Church is Israel according to the Spirit, from which is distinguished that Israel according to the flesh, which served in the shadows of sacrifices, by which was signified the single sacrifice which Israel according to the Spirit now offers, to whom it was said: 'Hear, my people, etc.' For he does not take young bulls from the house of this one. This one offers to God the sacrifice of praise, etc." And a little after: "In every place incense is offered to my name, etc., Malachi 1. For incense, which in Greek is thymiama, as John in the Apocalypse explains, is the prayers of the saints."

units.la: EVSEBIVS nobis obiectus loquitur de sacrificio laudis, ac propterea de spirituali sacrificio. Hæc enim sunt eius verba: Sacrificamus Deo altissimo sacrificium laudis, & paulo post: Memoriam illius magni sacrificij secundum ea quæ ab ipso tradita sunt mysteria celebrantes & gratias Deo pro salute nostra agentes, &c. Idē alibi locū hūc exponit de Incenso & sacrificio orationis quod Gentes per pias orationes summo Deo erant oblaturæ.
units.tr: Eusebius, who is thrown at us, speaks of a sacrifice of praise, and therefore of a spiritual sacrifice. His words are these: We offer to God Most High a sacrifice of praise, and a little later: celebrating the memory of that great sacrifice according to the mysteries delivered by him, and giving thanks to God for our salvation, etc. Elsewhere he explains the same passage as referring to incense and the sacrifice of prayer, which the Gentiles were to offer to the Most High God through pious prayers.

units.la: HIERONYMVS nobis obiectus idem etiam sensit: sic enim ille: Vt sciant carnalibus victimis spirituales victimas succedsuras, & nequaquam taurorum, hircorumque sanguinem, sed thymiama, hoc est, sanctorum orationes Domino offerendas. Sic etiam TERTVLLIANVS: In omni loco sacrificium mundum offeretur: scilicet simplex oratio de conscientia pura. & alibi: De spiritualibus vero sacrificiis addit dicens: Et in omni loco sacrificia munda offerentur nomini meo, dicit Dominus, & paulo ante: Sicut ipse per Malachiam dicit: Non recipiam sacrificium de manibus vestris, quoniam ab Oriente Sole usque ad Occidentem nomen meum clarificatum est in omnibus gentibus: & in omni loco offerentur sacrificia munda nomini meo. Item. in Psalmis Dauid dicit: Afferte Deo patria Gentium: indubitate quod in omni terra exire habebat praedicatio Apostolorum. Et alio in loco. Ab ortu Solis usque in Occasum nomen meum gloriatum est in nationibus, & in omni loco sacrificium nomini meo offertur & sacrificium mundu: Gloria scilicet relatio & benedictio, & laus & hymni. Sed non opus est pluribus: cum ipsorum Veterum, Prophetiam hanc de spiritualibus sacrificiis exponentium sententia palam ante omnium oculos constituta sit: adeo ut plane frigeat superior Pontificiorum obiectio.
units.tr: Jerome, who is thrown at us, held the same view. For he says: That they may know that spiritual sacrifices are to succeed carnal victims, and that not the blood of bulls and goats, but incense, that is, the prayers of the saints, is to be offered to the Lord. Tertullian likewise: In every place a pure sacrifice will be offered, namely simple prayer from a pure conscience. And elsewhere: Concerning spiritual sacrifices he adds, saying: And in every place pure sacrifices shall be offered to my name, saith the Lord. And a little before: As he himself says through Malachi: I will not accept the sacrifice from your hands, for from the rising of the sun even to the setting my name is glorified among all nations; and in every place pure sacrifices are offered to my name. Again, in the Psalms David says: Bring to God, O families of the Gentiles, undoubtedly because the preaching of the Apostles was to go out into all the earth. And in another place: From the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice: that is, the giving of glory and blessing, and praise and hymns. But there is no need for more. For since the opinion of the Fathers themselves, who explain this prophecy of spiritual sacrifices, is plainly set before the eyes of all, the foregoing objection of the Papists is wholly without force.

units.la: Obiectio 4.
units.tr: Objection 4.

units.la: Veteres passim Eucharistiam vocant sacrificium. Quare
units.tr: The ancients everywhere call the Eucharist a sacrifice. Therefore

units.la: Quare Missa sacrificium legitimum est.
units.tr: Therefore the Mass is a lawful sacrifice.

units.la: Antecedens non eget probatione: sic enim veteres identidem loqui solent, ut perspicuum est iis qui in eorum lectione versati sunt.
units.tr: The antecedent needs no proof, for the ancients commonly speak in this way, as is clear to those who have been versed in reading them.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Response.

units.la: Idem errores qui supra: tum in Consequente, tu etiam Antecedente. Quid enim, obsecro, commune habet Missa cum Coenae Dominicae sacramento? Adhaec (quod iam paulo ante diximus) considerandum est quo sensu Veteres S. Domini Coenam sacrificiu appellarint.
units.tr: The same errors as above, both in the consequent and in the antecedent. For what, I ask, does the Mass have in common with the sacrament of the Lord's Supper? Moreover, as we have already said a little earlier, we must consider in what sense the ancients called the Lord's Supper a sacrifice.

units.la: Primùm: quia in hoc mysterio fit commemoratio vnici illius sacrificij, quod pro nobis in cruce factum est. Atque haec commemoratio coniunctam habet gratiarum actionem: adeo vt sit sacrificium εὐχαριστικόν & gratiarum actionis: ac propterea inter spiritualia Christianorum sacrificia recensendum: teste Apostolo ad Hebr. Per ipsum, inquit, assiduè offeramus Deo sacrificium laudis, id est, fructum labiorum confitentium nomini eius.
units.tr: First, because in this mystery there is a commemoration of that one sacrifice which was made for us on the cross. And this commemoration has joined with it a thanksgiving, so that it is a eucharistic [εὐχαριστικόν] sacrifice of thanksgiving, and therefore is to be counted among the spiritual sacrifices of Christians, as the Apostle witnesses in Hebrews: Through him, he says, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.

units.la: Deinde quia in sacro hoc mysterio, siquidem à nobis cum vera fide, syncerisque animis celebretur, nos ipsos totos Deo consecramus: quod est spirituale sacrificium, nobis imprimis ab Apostolo commendatum his verbis: Precor vt sistatis corpora vestra hostiam viuam, sanctam, acceptam Deo, rationale cultum vestrum.
units.tr: Next, because in this holy mystery, provided it is celebrated by us with true faith and sincere hearts, we consecrate ourselves wholly to God, which is a spiritual sacrifice, commended to us above all by the Apostle in these words: I beseech you that you present your bodies a living, holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, your reasonable service.

units.la: Denique, quia id fuit olim in more positum, vt quum S. Coena celebraretur, tum fideles offerrent eleemosynas, quibus egenis fratribus subuenirent: quod est etiam spiritualis sacrificij genus ita docente Apostolo, Beneficentiæ & communicationis ne obliuiscimini, talibus enim victimis delectatur Deus. Huc veteres respexisse, cum Eucharistiam sacrificium appellarunt, satis perspicuum esse potest ex ipso vocabulo Eucharistiæ, quod significat gratiarum actionem. Quare qui sacrificium Eucharistiæ dicit, ille dicit sacrificium gratiarum actionis. Sed præstat ex infinitis propè veterum testimoniis quaedam excerpere, ex quibus eorum sententia fiat etiamnum dilucidior.
units.tr: Finally, because it was once the custom that, when the Lord's Supper was celebrated, the faithful would also offer alms, by which they might help needy brethren; this too is a kind of spiritual sacrifice, as the Apostle teaches: Do not forget beneficence and fellowship, for with such victims God is pleased. That the ancients had this in view when they called the Eucharist a sacrifice can be quite clear from the very word Eucharist, which means thanksgiving. Therefore whoever calls it the sacrifice of the Eucharist calls it the sacrifice of thanksgiving. But it is better to select a few out of almost countless testimonies of the ancients, by which their opinion will become clearer still.

units.la: CYPRIANVS. Quia passionis eius mentionem in sacrificiis omnibus facimus (passio est enim Domini sacrificium quod offerimus) nihil aliud quam quod ipse fecit facere debemus.
units.tr: Cyprian: Because we make mention of his passion in all our sacrifices (for the passion of the Lord is the sacrifice which we offer), we ought to do nothing else than what he himself did.

units.la: CHRYSOSTOMVS. Si mortuus Iesus non est: cuius symbolum ac signum hoc sacrificium est? Idem: Quod pro Iudæorum salute aliquando faciebat, temporibus, locisque ac festiuitatibus variis in memoriam illos suorum beneficiorum reducens: id nunc quidem magno cum cumulo est operatus in nobis ipso genere sacrificij ad ingenos pro beneficiis suis gratiarum incitans actionem. Idem: Offerimus quidem sed ad recordationem facientes mortis eius.
units.tr: Chrysostom: If Jesus is not dead, of what symbol and sign is this sacrifice? The same: He who once did this for the salvation of the Jews, bringing them back in memory of his benefits at various times, places and festivals, has now, by this very kind of sacrifice, worked far more abundantly in us, stirring us up to great thanksgiving for his benefits. The same: We indeed offer, but in remembrance of his death.

units.la: AMBROSIVS ex Chrysostomo: Nonne per singulos dies offerimus? offerimus quidem, sed recorrecordationem facientes mortis eius: & una est hæc hostia, non multa. Quomodo una est, & non multa? Quia semel oblata est in sancta sanctorum. Hoc autem sacrificium exemplar illius est, &c. Hoc quod facimus, in commemorationem fit eius quod factum est. Hoc enim facite, inquit, in mei commemorationem. Non aliud sacrificium sicut Pontifex: sed ipsum semper offerimus: magis autem recordationem sacrificij operamur.
units.tr: Ambrose, following Chrysostom: Do we not offer every day? We indeed offer, but making remembrance of his death; and this is one victim, not many. How is it one and not many? Because it was offered once for all in the holy of holies. This sacrifice, moreover, is an image of that one, etc. What we do is done in commemoration of what was done. For, he says, do this in remembrance of me. We do not offer another sacrifice as the high priest does, but we always offer the same; or rather we perform a remembrance of the sacrifice.

units.la: AVGVSTINVS: Sacrificium laudis honorificabit me Psal. 49. Quod est autem sacratius laudis sacrificium, quàm in actione gratiarum? Unde maiores agenda sunt Deo gratiæ, quàm pro ipsius gratia per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum? Quod totum fideles in Ecclesia sacrificio sciunt, &c. Idem: Nonne semel immolatus est Christus in seipso? & tamen in sacrificio non solum per omnes Paschæ solennitates, sed omni die populis immolatur. Nec utique mentitur qui interrogatus, eum responderit immolari. Si enim sacramenta quandam similitudinem earum rerum quarum sacramenta sunt, non haberent: omnino sacramenta non essent, &c. Idem: Firmissimè tene & nullatenus dubites unigenitum Dei verbum carnem factum se pro nobis obtulisse sacrificium, & hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis: cui nunc cum Patre & Spiritu Sancto sacrificium panis & vini in fide & charitate sancta Ecclesia catholica per universum orbem. M 2 terra offerre non cessat. In carnalibus victimis figuratio fuit carnis Christi quam pro peccatis nostris fuerat oblaturus. In ipso autem sacrificio gratiarum actio atque commemoratio est carnis Christi quam pro nobis obtulit, &c. Idem, Hoc est sacrificium Christianorum: multi unum corpus sumus in Christo: quod etiam sacramento altaris fidelibus noto frequentat Ecclesia: vbi ei demonstratur, quod in ea oblatione quam offert, ipsa offeratur. Idem, Sacrificium laudis glorificabit me Psal. 49. Huius sacrificij caro & sanguis ante aduentum Christi per victimas similitudinum promittebatur: in passione Christi per ipsam veritatem reddebatur: post ascensum Christi per sacramentum memoriae celebratur.
units.tr: Augustine: The sacrifice of praise shall glorify me, Psalm 49. But what sacrifice of praise is more sacred than thanksgiving? Whence greater thanks must be given to God than for his grace through our Lord Jesus Christ? All this the faithful know in the sacrifice of the Church, etc. The same: Has not Christ been sacrificed once in himself? And yet in the sacrifice he is sacrificed not only at all the Easter solemnities but every day to the peoples. Nor does he lie who, being asked, answers that he is sacrificed. For if sacraments had no likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all, etc. The same: Hold most firmly, and never doubt, that the only-begotten Word of God, made flesh, offered himself for us as a sacrifice and a victim of sweet odour to God; to whom now, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church throughout the whole world in faith and holy charity does not cease to offer the sacrifice of bread and wine. In the carnal victims there was a figure of the flesh of Christ which he was to offer for our sins. But in the sacrifice itself there is the giving of thanks and the remembrance of the flesh of Christ which he offered for us, etc. The same: This is the sacrifice of Christians: we, being many, are one body in Christ; which the Church also frequents in the sacrament of the altar, known to the faithful, where it is shown to her that in that offering which she makes, she herself is offered. The same: The sacrifice of praise shall glorify me, Psalm 49. The flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised before the coming of Christ through victims of likeness; in the passion of Christ it was rendered through the truth itself; after the ascension of Christ it is celebrated through the sacrament of remembrance.

units.la: Evsebivs. Memoriam illius magni sacrificij celebrantes, &c. Verum quid pluribus recensendis immoramur? Saltem audiant Pontificij Magistrum suum Petrum Lombardum, quo vno ipsorum scholae personat, ita quaestionem hanc definientem.
units.tr: Eusebius: celebrating the memory of that great sacrifice, etc. But why do we linger in recounting more? At least let the Papists hear their own master, Peter Lombard, on whom alone the schools of their party resound, defining this question thus.

units.la: Quaeritur: si quod gerit sacerdos, proprie dicatur sacrificium, vel immolatio: &, Si Christus quotidie immoletur: vel semel tantum immolatus sit. Ad hoc breuiter dici potest: Illud quod offertur & consecratur a sacerdote vocari sacrificium & oblationem: quia memoria est & repraesentatio veri sacrificij & sanctae immolationis facta in ara crucis. Et, semel Christus mortuus est in cruce, ibique immolatus est in semetipso: quotidie autem immolatur in sacramento, quia in sacramento recordatio
units.tr: It is asked: whether what the priest does is properly called a sacrifice or an immolation; and whether Christ is immolated daily, or was immolated only once. To this it can briefly be said: that which is offered and consecrated by the priest is called a sacrifice and an oblation, because it is a memorial and representation of the true sacrifice and holy immolation made on the altar of the cross. And: Christ died once on the cross, and was immolated there in himself; but he is immolated daily in the sacrament, because in the sacrament there is a remembrance

units.la: Sent. li. 4. dist. 12. &c vid. Can. Semel immolatus & Can. In Christo. De Consecr. dist. 2 cordatio fit illius quod factum est semel. Sic Lo-bardus breuiter (vt ille quidem ait) & verbis paucissimis, profusam Pontificiorum de reali suo sacrificio loquacitatem redarguit. Iaquod diximus veteres censuisse, in sacra Coena nos totos esse Deo, spirituali sacrificio offerendos, non eget probatione: neque id Pontificij in dubium revocant: itemque de oblationibus in vsum pauperum olim fieri solitis, plura non sunt dicenda, quandoquidem ea de re testes audiuimus Irenæum & Ambrosium. Nec puto oblationem (Offertorium vocant) sacerdotibus Pontificiis displicere: non iam pauperibus erogandam (qui mos veterum fuit) sed priuatis sacrificulorum commodis cessuram. Itaque legem hanc in sua Decreta retulerunt. Omnis Christianus procuret ad Missarum solennia aliquid Deo offerre, & ducere ad memoriam quod Deus per Moysen dixit: Non apparebis in conspectu meo vacuus. Hæc Gregorius VII. vbi glossator ait, eas oblationes esse ex debito exigendas, ad eásque dandas Parochianos cogendos esse. O tempora! En igitur quò redierint veterum oblationes quibus suam testati sunt erga pauperes benignitatem. Sed de his ac de tota quidem superiori obiectione, hactenus.
units.tr: Sentences, book 4, distinction 12; see also the canons Semel immolatus and In Christo, De Consecratione, distinction 2: of that which was done once. Thus Lombard, briefly (as he himself says) and in very few words, refutes the lavish talkativeness of the Papists about their real sacrifice. That we have said the ancients held that in the Lord's Supper we are to offer ourselves wholly to God as a spiritual sacrifice needs no proof, nor do the Papists call this into doubt. Likewise, concerning the offerings once customarily made for the use of the poor, there is no need to say more, since we have heard Irenaeus and Ambrose as witnesses on this matter. Nor do I think the offering (which they call the Offertory) displeases the Papist priests, which is no longer to be distributed to the poor (which was the custom of the ancients), but is to go to the private advantage of the little sacrificers. And so they have recorded this law in their Decrees: Every Christian should take care to offer something to God at the solemnities of the Masses, and to bring to mind what God said through Moses: You shall not appear before my face empty. Gregory VII says these things, where the glossator says that these offerings are to be exacted as a due, and that parishioners are to be compelled to give them. O the times! Behold, then, to what the offerings of the ancients, by which they attested their kindness toward the poor, have come back. But of this, and of the whole of the foregoing objection, so far.

units.la: Obiectio 5.
units.tr: Objection 5.

units.la: Hieronymus eos refellit qui locum Danielis de tollendo iugi sacrificio ad Antiochi tempora re-
units.tr: Jerome refutes those who took the passage in Daniel about the removal of the continual sacrifice to refer to the time of Antiochus

units.la: Cā. Omnis Christian. de Consec. dist. 1.
units.tr: Decretum, Omnis Christianus, De Consecratione, dist. 1.

units.la: In cap. 12. Danielis. ferabant:eumque exponit de Antichristo . Ergo tenet consequentia supra suo loco propositu:locum Danielis esse de Missae sacrificio exponendum.
units.tr: On Daniel, chapter 12. and expounds it of Antichrist. Therefore the inference stated above in its place holds: the passage in Daniel must be expounded of the sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: De Prophetia Danielis ac de iugi sacrificio suo loco disseruimus. Ad Hieronymi sententiam quod attinet: posisim ego vicissim testem producere Chrysostomum, Danielis prophetiam de Antiocho verbis clarissimis exponentem: & iuge sacrificium ad legales caeremonias referentem. Sic enim ille, Erat mos Iudaeis & vesperi & sub auroram & singulo quoque die sacrificium offerre Deo. Atque hac de causa sacrificium illud Entelechismum, id est, assiduitatem, sive continuationem vocabant. Itaque veniens Antiochus hunc morem sustulit. Caeterum, liceat quidem Hieronymo & plerisque aliis autoribus existimare, Antiochum fuisse typum Antichristi & in hunc etiam quadrare quae de illo dicta sunt: Sed nihil propterea Pontificiorum sententiae video accedere. Nec enim Hieronymus verbum vllum facit de isto Missae sacrificio: sed tantum ait Antichristo saevienente cultum Dei interruptum iri. Verba Hieronymi haec sunt: A tempore ἐντελεχισμὸς, quod nos interpretati sumus iuge sacrificium, quando Antichristus orbe obtinens Dei cultum interdixerit, &c. Ex quibus perspicuum esse poterit, etiam ipso Hieronymo iudice (quem illi testem excitarunt) locum Danielis commentitio Missae sacrificio ficio non patrocinari.
units.tr: We have discussed the prophecy of Daniel and the continual sacrifice in their proper place. As for Jerome's opinion, I in turn may produce a witness, Chrysostom, who expounds Daniel's prophecy clearly as referring to Antiochus and relates the continual sacrifice to the legal ceremonies. For he says: "It was the custom of the Jews to offer sacrifice to God both in the evening and at dawn, every single day. For this reason they called that sacrifice entelechismus [ἐντελεχισμός], that is, continuity or perpetuity. So when Antiochus came, he abolished this custom." Yet, although Jerome and many other authors may think that Antiochus was a type of Antichrist and that what is said of the latter also fits him, I see that nothing in this supports the opinion of the Papists. For Jerome says nothing at all about this sacrifice of the Mass; he only says that when Antichrist rages, the worship of God will be interrupted. Jerome's words are these: "From the time of entelechismos [ἐντελεχισμὸς], which we have translated as the continual sacrifice, when Antichrist, holding the world, shall forbid the worship of God, etc." From these words it can be clear that, even by Jerome's own judgment (whom they have brought forward as a witness), the passage in Daniel does not lend support to the fabricated sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: Obiectio 6.
units.tr: Objection 6.

units.la: Quod vniuersa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis in-ftitutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi Apo-ftolica authoritate traditum rectissimè creditur.
units.tr: What the whole Church holds, and what has not been instituted by Councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down only by apostolic authority.

units.la: Sacrificium Missæ est eiusmodi.
units.tr: The sacrifice of the Mass is of this kind.

units.la: Quare sacrificium Missæ non nisi Apostolica authoritate traditum, rectissimè creditur: & vi Consequentis, legitimum est.
units.tr: Therefore the sacrifice of the Mass, handed down only by apostolic authority, is rightly believed; and by force of the conclusion it is lawful.

units.la: Maior est ex Augustino deprompta, Minorem ipsa experientia comprobat.
units.tr: The major premise is taken from Augustine; the minor is confirmed by experience itself.

units.la: Responsio.
units.tr: Reply.

units.la: Maiorem executio. Truncatus est locus. Agebatur de Pædobaptismo: cuius probationem siquis ex Scriptura postulauerit: Etsi, inquit Augustinus, quod vniuersa tenet Ecclesia, nec Conciliis institutum, sed semper retentū est, non nisi Apostolica authoritate traditum rectissimè creditur: tamen veraciter continere possumus quid valeat in paruulis Baptismi sacramentum, ex Circuncifione, &c. Sequantur ergo Pontificij testem suum Augustinum, qui ne ipsa quidem consuetudine, inde vsque ab Apostolorum temporibus semper vsurpata contentus, libenter recurrit ad Scriptu-ræ firmamenta. Nimirum non pro consuetudine, sed pro veritate certabat Augustinus, cuius quidem veritatis alibi, rationem inuincibilem esse affirmauit: quippe (vt ille ipse docuit) in sacris libris iuuestigandam. Admittimus igitur quæ dixit & vt dixit Augustinus: Ea quæ semper vsurpata fuerunt in Ecclesia Christiana ab Apostolorum temporibus & quæ firmamentum habet in Scriptura: ea fuisse ab Apostolis tradita.
units.tr: I grant the major premise, but its application is wrong, since the passage has been cut short. The subject under discussion was infant baptism, and if anyone demands proof of it from Scripture, Augustine says: "Although what the whole Church holds, and what has not been instituted by Councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down only by apostolic authority, we can nevertheless truly show from circumcision what power the sacrament of baptism has in little children, etc." Let the Papists therefore follow their witness Augustine, who, not content even with custom always practised from the times of the Apostles, gladly has recourse to the supports of Scripture. Clearly Augustine was contending not for custom but for truth, and he affirmed elsewhere that the reason for this truth is unconquerable, since (as he himself taught) it is to be sought in the sacred books. So we admit what Augustine said, and as he said it: those things which have always been practised in the Christian Church from the times of the Apostles, and which have support in Scripture, were handed down by the Apostles.

units.la: Minor plane falsa est. Nec enim verum est Missæ sacrificium ab Apostolorum temporibus ad hęc vsque tempora perdurasse: cùm Apostoli & veteres ipsi Doctores sacrificiū Missæ ne nominent quidem: & ex historia satis constet, à multis ac variis authoribus Missæ sacrificium fuisse consarcinatum. Nec etiam verum est, ipsum habere vllū in Scriptura firmamentum. Quamobrem vt Augustinum ex Augustino ipso dir gamus: Afferamus, (inquit in illa ipsa disputatione) diuinam stateram de Scripturis sanctis & in illis quid sit grauius, appendamus.
units.tr: The minor premise is plainly false. For it is not true that the sacrifice of the Mass has lasted from the times of the Apostles down to our own: the Apostles and the early teachers themselves do not even name the sacrifice of the Mass, and history makes it quite clear that the sacrifice of the Mass was patched together by many and various authors. Nor is it true that it has any support in Scripture. Therefore, to turn Augustine against himself, let us in his own words in that same disputation: "Let us bring forward the divine balance from the holy Scriptures, and weigh in it what is heavier."

units.la: Quæ cùm itasint, cuiuis, vt spero, manifestū esse potest, nullius esse ponderis ea quæ Pontificij è veterum scriptis argumenta deprom serunt, tum quia fides nostra non hominū, sed solius S. Scripturæ authoritate niti debet: tum quia veterum sententias in alienum sensum detorserunt, vt eas suis commentis addicerent. Verumenimuero vt hanc Pontificiorum iniectam maculam ipsi veteres, sua potius quàm nostra manu, abstergere videantur: Audiamus quidnam illi de Christianorum sacrificiis docuerint cum ipso Dei verbo consentaneum.
units.tr: Since these things stand thus, it can be plain, I hope, to anyone that the arguments the Papists draw from the writings of the ancients are of no weight, both because our faith ought to rest on the authority of Holy Scripture alone and not of men, and because they have twisted the opinions of the ancients into a foreign sense in order to bend them to their own inventions. Yet, so that the ancients themselves may seem to wipe away this stain which the Papists have fastened on them, let us rather with their own hand hear what they taught about the sacrifices of Christians that agrees with the very Word of God.

units.la: CAPVT
units.tr: Chapter

units.la: CAPVT 6.
units.tr: CHAPTER 6.

units.la: VVM Augustinus aduersus CresconiumDonatistā Theologicè disputaret, Cypriani scriptis ad confirmatione sui erroris abutentem: Literas, inquit, Cypriani, non vt Canonicas habeo, sed eas ex Canonicis considero: & quod in eis Diuinarum scripturarum authoritati congruit, cum laude eius accipio: quod autem non congruit, cum pace eius respuo. Sic peritus ille Theologus accuratas ac Theologicas disputatio-nes distinguebat à probabili ratione differendi.Nos igitur ipsum Dei verbū sequentes, & hac quidem in re, Augustini vestigiis insistentes, ea quae veteres tradiderunt, ex Canonicis literis consideramus, & quae Diuinarum Scripturam authoritati cōgruunt, cum eorum laude accipimus: quae vero non congruunt, cum ipsorum veterum pace respuimus. Hoc autem si in omnibus capitibus religionis Christianae, quanto magis in praecipuo hoc argumento faciendum est, vbi agitur de vero sacrificio noui Testamenti? Quamobrem cum pij veteres saepe docuerint Christi sacrificium in cruce pro nobis semel factum, esse vnicum sacrificium noui Testamenti proprie dictum, propitiatorium pro peccatis nostris, cuius quidem semel peracti virtus & efficacitas sit perpetua: Christianorũ autẽ sacrificia non realia, externáque, sed esse spiritualia: hanc veterũ sententiam, Scripturarum authoritati congruentem, nos cum eorũ laude accipere, te stabimur subiectis aliquot Doctorum veterũ testimoniis: ex quibus erũt dirigeda & ex poneda, si quę forte in aliis eorũ scriptis, de sacrificio, minus accuratè dicta reperiatur.
units.tr: When Augustine was disputing theologically against Cresconius the Donatist, who abused the writings of Cyprian to confirm his error, he said: "I do not hold the letters of Cyprian as canonical, but I weigh them against the canonical books. What agrees with the authority of the divine Scriptures I accept with praise for him; what does not agree I reject with his leave." In this way that skilled theologian distinguished accurate, theological disputation from probable reasoning about opinions. We, then, following the Word of God itself, and in this matter treading in Augustine's footsteps, weigh what the ancients have handed down by the canonical writings. What agrees with the authority of the divine Scriptures we accept with their praise; what does not agree we reject with the leave of the ancients themselves. If this must be done in all the articles of the Christian religion, how much more must it be done in this principal subject, where the true sacrifice of the New Testament is treated? Therefore, although the godly ancients often taught that the sacrifice of Christ, once made for us on the cross, is the one sacrifice of the New Testament properly so called, a propitiation for our sins, whose power and efficacy, once accomplished, is perpetual; and that the sacrifices of Christians are not real and external but spiritual, we shall set out, subjoined, some testimonies of the ancient teachers, so that we may accept this opinion of the ancients, which agrees with the authority of the Scriptures, with their praise. From these, whatever is perhaps said less accurately about sacrifice in other of their writings shall be corrected and set aside.

units.la: TERTVLLIANVS. Vade, ostende te sacerdoti & offer munus quod praecepit Moyses Matth.8. Argumenta figurata vt puta Prophetæ legis adhuc in suis imaginibus tuebatur: quæ significabant hominem quondam peccatore verbo mox Dei emaculatum offerre debere munus Deo apud templum, orationem scilicet & actione gratiarum apud Ecclesiam per Christum Iesum catholicum Patris sacerdotem. Idem. Quod non terrenis sed spiritualibus sacrificiis Deo litandũ sit, ita legimus vt scriptum est: Cor contribulatum hostia est Dei: & alibi Sacrifica Deo sacrificiũ laudis. Idem. Fides tua te saluam fecit: quia intellexerat verâ se Deo omnipotenti oblationem, gratiarum scilicet actionem apud verum templum & verum Pontificem eius Christum facere debere. Idem, Sacrificamus pro salute Imperatoris: sed Deo nostro & ipsius: sed quomodo præcepit Deus, pura prece.
units.tr: TERTULLIAN. "Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded" (Matth. 8.). The prophet of the law, for instance, still kept to the figurative arguments in its images, which signified that a man once a sinner, now cleansed by the word of God, ought to offer a gift to God at the temple: namely prayer and thanksgiving in the Church, through Jesus Christ, the Catholic priest of the Father. The same author: "That sacrifices are to be offered to God not of earthly but of spiritual things, we read as it is written: 'A contrite heart is a sacrifice to God'; and elsewhere, 'Offer to God the sacrifice of praise.'" The same: "Your faith has saved you," because he had understood that he ought to make a true offering to the true almighty God, namely thanksgiving, at the true temple and before its true High Priest, Christ. The same: "We sacrifice for the safety of the Emperor, but to our God and his; yet as God has commanded, with pure prayer."

units.la: IRENAEVS. Sic & ideo nos quoq; offerre vult munus ad altare frequenter sine intermissione. Est ergo altare in cælis: illuc enim preces nostræ & oblationes nostræ diriguntur & ad templum. plum: quemadmodũ Ioannes in Apocalypsi ait, Et apertum est templum Dei & Tabernaculum: Ecce enim, inquit, Tabernaculum Dei in quo habitabit cum hominibus.
units.tr: IRENAEUS. So also God wishes us to offer a gift frequently, without intermission, at the altar. There is therefore an altar in heaven; for our prayers and our offerings are directed there, and also to the temple, as John says in the Apocalypse: "And the temple of God and the tabernacle was opened. For behold," he says, "the tabernacle of God in which he will dwell with men."

units.la: IVSTINVS MARTYR. Supplicationes simul & gratiarum actiones quæ à dignis peragúntur solas perfectas esse, & Deo charas vis-simas, ipse quoque affirmauerim: has vero solas facere Christiani didicerunt, &c. Idem. Cui citra intermissionem mastamus hostiam laudis, & vt Deo, preces synceras libamus, & fragrantem operum bonorum odorem sacrificamus &c.
units.tr: JUSTIN MARTYR. "I myself would affirm that supplications together with thanksgivings, offered by the worthy, alone are perfect and most dear to God; and Christians have learned to make these alone, etc." The same: "To him we offer without ceasing the sacrifice of praise, and as to God we pour out sincere prayers, and we sacrifice the fragrant odour of good works, etc."

units.la: BASILIVS. Qui ex semine Aaronis consecrabantur exclusi sunt, vt istis succederet sacerdos secundùm ordinẽ Melchisedec. Non iã illud iuge sacrificiũ, aut victimæ continuò repetitæ, &c. Vna enim hostia Christus, & quæ pro eius confessione celebratur sanctorum mortificatio: vna aspersio, nempe lauacrũ regenerationis: vna expiatio peccati, nimirũ sanguis ille pro salute mundi effusus. Idem. Quo mihi, inquit, multitudine victimarũ vestrarũ? Repudiata tali multitudine, vnam requirit hostiã, nimirũ vt quisque se conciliet & offerat Deo, seipsum sistens Deo in hostiã viuente per rationale obsequium, immolans Deo sacrificium laudationis: quandoquidem multitudo illarum legalium victimarum explosa est. Vna in hoc seculorum fine approbata est, semel oblata in abolitionem peccati. Agnus enim Dei abstulit peccatum mundi, seipsum offerens oblationem & hostiam in odorem suauitatis.
units.tr: BASIL. "Those who were consecrated from the seed of Aaron were set aside, so that a priest after the order of Melchizedek might succeed them. Not that perpetual sacrifice, or victims constantly repeated, etc. For Christ is one sacrifice, and the mortification of the saints, celebrated in confession of him, is one; one sprinkling, namely the washing of regeneration; one expiation of sin, that blood poured out for the salvation of the world." The same: "What," he says, "do I want with the multitude of your victims?" Having rejected such a multitude, he asks for one sacrifice: namely that each man should reconcile himself and offer himself to God, presenting himself to God as a living victim through a reasonable service, offering to God the sacrifice of praise; since the multitude of those legal victims has been cast out. One has been approved at the end of the ages, offered once for the abolition of sin. For the Lamb of God has taken away the sin of the world, offering himself as an oblation and a victim for a sweet-smelling savour.

units.la: GREGOR. NAZIANZENVS. Magna illa & quantum ad primam naturam immaculatis bilis victima legalibus sacrificiis immixta est: illa, inquam, non exigua cuiusdam partis orbis terrarum, nec ad exiguum tempus, sed totius mundi, nec vnquam intermoritura expiatio. Idem. Deo super altari superno cum coelestibus choris sacrificium laudis immolemus: penetremus primum velamen, ad secundum accedamus, omnibus horis nosmetipsos Deo immolantes, &c. Idem. Prima sapientia est vita proba & honesta, Deoque perpurgata, Deo, inquam, purissimo & a nobis solum purgationis sacrificium requirente, quod quidem cor contritum & laudis sacrificium & nouam in Christo creaturam, idque genus nominibus appellare, Scriptura sacra familiare est.
units.tr: GREGORY NAZIANZEN. "That great victim, spotless as regards its first nature, was mingled with the legal sacrifices: that expiation, I say, not of some small part of the lands of the earth, nor for a short time, but of the whole world, and one that will never perish." The same: "Let us offer to God, upon the supreme altar, with the heavenly choirs, the sacrifice of praise; let us first penetrate the veil, let us approach the second, offering ourselves to God at all hours, etc." The same: "The first wisdom is an upright and honest life, thoroughly purged for God, for God, I say, most pure, who from us requires only the sacrifice of purification; which the contrite heart, the sacrifice of praise, and the new creature in Christ are; and Holy Scripture is accustomed to call them by these names."

units.la: EPIPHANIVS. Num quadraginta annis sacrificium mihi obtulistis in deserto? &c. vt discerent quod Deus per aduentum Christi suum omnem sacrificiorum vsum tolleret, vno sacrificio omnia quae antea fuerunt, comp'ente ac perficiente, quod est sacrificium & victima Christi. Nam Pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus.
units.tr: EPIPHANIUS. "Did you offer me sacrifice for forty years in the wilderness? etc." That they might learn that God, by the coming of his Christ, would abolish all use of sacrifices, completing and perfecting by one sacrifice all that had been before, which is the sacrifice and victim Christ. For "our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed."

units.la: CHRYSOSTOMVS. Postquam dixit sacrificium & oblationem noluisti, addidit, corpus autem adaptasti mihi: quoniam ostendit aliud inductum sacrificium: & hoc ipsum interpretans Paulus dixit: Per oblationem hanc sanctificati sumus in voluntate Christi: si enim sanguis taurorum, hircorum, & cinis victimae aspersus inquinat quinatos sanctificat ad carnis emundationem: quanto magis sanguis Iesu Christi, &c. Itaque quod illud sacrificium antiquatum est & aliud in eius locum inductum, satis ex his demonstratum est. Idem. Christus non semper crucifigitur, Vnum enim pro peccatis nostris tulit sacrificium, sed semper per illud nos purgat. Idem. Christus perfectus est, nunquam peccat, semper viuit, cur pro nobis offerret multa sacrificia? &c. Non est aliud sacrificium: vnum nos purgauit: post illud, ignis & gehenna. Propterea sursum atque deorsum reuoluit Apostolus dicens vnum sacerdotem, vnum sacrificium: nequis putans multa esse, sine timore delinquat. Idem. In coelis habemus sacrarium: in coelis sacerdotem: in coelis hostiam: talia etiam nos offeramus sacrificia quae in illo sanctuario possint offerri. Non iam pecudes, vel boues: omnia haec soluta sunt, & pro eis introductum est rationabile obsequium. Quid autem est rationabile obsequium? quae per animam & secundum spiritum offeruntur. Spiritus est, inquit, Deus: & eos qui adorant eum, in spiritu & veritate oportet adorare. Quicquid non indiget corpore: quicquid non indiget instrumentis, neque locis in quibus quidem est Pontifex: vt est mansuetudo, temperantia, misericordia, patientia, longanimitas, animi modestia, &c. Vides alia quidem discedentia, alia succedentia sacrificia. Haec igitur offeramus. Illa quidem diuitiarum sunt: haec virtutis: illa externa, extrinsecus: ista intrinsecus, &c.
units.tr: CHRYSOSTOM. "After he said, 'Sacrifice and offering you did not desire,' he added, 'but a body you have prepared for me'; since this shows that another sacrifice has been introduced; and Paul, interpreting this very thing, said: 'By this offering we have been sanctified in the will of Christ'; for if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled, defile the defiled, they sanctify to the cleansing of the flesh; how much more the blood of Jesus Christ, etc." Therefore it has been sufficiently demonstrated from these things that that sacrifice has been abolished and another introduced in its place. The same: Christ is not crucified continually. For "he has borne one sacrifice for our sins," but he always cleanses us by that one. The same: Christ is perfect, never sins, always lives; why would he offer many sacrifices for us? etc. There is no other sacrifice: one has cleansed us; after that, there is fire and hell. Therefore the Apostle turns us back and forth, saying: one priest, one sacrifice; lest anyone, thinking there are many, sin without fear. The same: In heaven we have a sanctuary, in heaven a priest, in heaven a victim. Let us also offer such sacrifices as can be offered in that sanctuary. Not now sheep or oxen: all these are loosed, and in their place a reasonable service has been introduced. What, then, is a reasonable service? Those things which are offered through the soul and according to the spirit. "God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth." Whatever does not need a body, whatever does not need instruments or places (in which, indeed, the High Priest is): such as gentleness, temperance, mercy, patience, longsuffering, modesty of mind, etc. You see that some sacrifices are passing away, and others are succeeding. Let us offer these. The former belong to riches, these to virtue; the former are external, outward; these are inward, etc.

units.la: CYRILLVS. An ignoras tibi quoque, id est, omni Ecclesiæ Dei & fidelium populo sacerdotium datum? Audi quomodo Petrus dicit de fidelibus: Genus, inquit, electum, regale sacerdotium, gens sancta, populus acquisitionis. Habes ergo sacerdotium, quia gens sacerdotalis es, & ideo offerre debes Deo hostiã laudis, hostiam orationum, hostiam misericordiæ, hostiam pudicitiæ, hostiam iustitiæ, hostiã sanctitatis. Idem. Stat ergo etiam nunc verus noster Pontifex Christus & implere vult manus suas incenso compositό minuto: & ab vnaquaque Ecclesia quæ sub cœlo est considerat quid offeratur: quàm integrè incensum suum diligenterque componat, quàm minutum id faciat: id est, quomodo vnusquisq; nostrum opera sua ordinet & quomodo sensum ac verba Scripturarum spirituali explanatione discutiat, &c.
units.tr: CYRILLUS. "Do you not know that the priesthood has been given to you as well, that is, to the whole Church of God and the people of the faithful? Hear how Peter speaks of the faithful: 'a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition.' You have therefore a priesthood, because you are a priestly nation, and so you ought to offer to God the sacrifice of praise, the sacrifice of prayers, the sacrifice of mercy, the sacrifice of chastity, the sacrifice of righteousness, the sacrifice of holiness." The same: "So even now our true High Priest, Christ, stands and wishes to fill his hands with incense compounded finely; and he considers from each Church that is under heaven what is offered: how entirely and diligently he compounds his incense, how finely he makes it; that is, how each of us arranges his works, and how he examines the sense and words of the Scriptures by spiritual explanation, etc."

units.la: Idem. Sacrificamus nunc multò melius quàm illi olim. Descendit enim cœlitus non sensibilis ignis sed ex Patre per Filium Spiritus Sanctus illustrans Ecclesiam: adhibemus autem & sacrificia, spiritualia scilicet, & mentalia. Nam illi quidem offerebant Deo boues, oues, turtures & columbas, & ex fructibus & similam oleo sparsam & lagana & thura. Nos autè tam crasso ministerio relicto præceptum habemus vt tenue ac spirituale & subtile perficiamus. Offerimus enim in odorem suavitatis Deo virtutes omnigenas, fidem, spem, charitatem, iustitiam, continentiam, perpetuas laudes & alias virtutes. Illud enim sacrificium minimè carnale, simplicem
units.tr: Idem. We now sacrifice far better than they did of old. For the Holy Spirit comes down from heaven, not as a visible fire, but from the Father through the Son, illuminating the Church. We also have sacrifices, spiritual and mental ones. They indeed offered to God oxen, sheep, turtledoves and pigeons, and from the fruits, flour sprinkled with oil, cakes and incense. But we, having left behind such a gross ministry, have a command to perform one that is fine, spiritual and refined. For we offer to God, as a fragrant aroma, virtues of every kind: faith, hope, love, righteousness, self-control, unending praises and other virtues. For that sacrifice, not at all carnal but simple

units.la: Sacrificia Christianorũ nõ sunt crassa & externa, sed spiritualia: cuiusmodi sunt virtutes, gratiarum actio &c. cem & secundum naturam incorporeum decet Deum, & mentalis fragrantiæ oblationes sunt veræ honestæ vitæ modi.
units.tr: The sacrifices of Christians are not gross and external but spiritual, such as virtues, thanksgiving and the like, and it befits God, who is incorporeal by nature, that the offerings be of the mind, and that they be true modes of an honourable life, a fragrance of the mind.

units.la: HIERONYMVS. Nunquid manducabo carnes taurorum? &c.Psal.49. Quum veteris legis cæremonias resumisset, transit ad Evangelicam puritatem, & quid pro his cupiat ostendit. Immola Deo sacrificium laudis, inquit. Idē. Historiam Ionæ ad Christum & ad vocationem Gentium referens: Ante Domini Passionem timentes clamauerunt ad Deos suos. Post passionem eius, Dominum timent, venerantur & colunt, & immolauerunt hostias quas certè iuxta literam in mediis fluctibus non habebant: sed quia sacrificium Deo spiritus contribulatus est, &c. Ionas in mari fugitiuus, naufragus, mortuus saluat naviculam fluctuantem, salvat Ethnicos in diuersas prius sententias mundi errore iactatos. Ex quo ostenditur sedari non posse naufragium, nisi morte fugitiui. Idem. Et immolabo in tabernaculo eius hostiam iubilationis, Psalm.26.
